    #159079. Why Evergreen Shrubs Have Black or Brown Leaves in December – and When You Should Act Fast if You Spot This Leaf Damage

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1602 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Evergreen Shrubs Have Black or Brown Leaves in December – and When You Should Act Fast if You Spot This Leaf Damage

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1602 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Evergreen shrubs are workhorses in the garden, providing year-round green foliage, privacy hedging, and focal points in beds.
    • It has been revealed that the mild fall in many areas this year allowed many shrubs to delay dormancy and even put out fresh growth.
    • Blackened or brown evergreen leaf tips don't necessarily mean your shrubs are dying, but they are cause for concern and a clear sign you need to prepare your garden for winter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Evergreen shrubs are workhorses in the garden, providing year-round green foliage, privacy hedging, and focal points in beds. They're the backbone of a winter garden, which is why it's so disappointing to find brown or black leaf tips on a hebe, photinia, choisya, arborvitae or other evergreens after the first cold snap. And this year, evergreen shrubs with dead leaf tips are a problem many gardeners are facing as temperatures drop.

    It has been revealed that the mild fall in many areas this year allowed many shrubs to delay dormancy and even put out fresh growth. Without the time to build cold resistance before winter weather arrives, evergreen foliage is left vulnerable to leaf damage.

    Blackened or brown evergreen leaf tips don't necessarily mean your shrubs are dying, but they are cause for concern and a clear sign you need to prepare your garden for winter. Understanding what's caused the damage is crucial so you know what to do next to save your beloved evergreen shrubs. So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your evergreen shrubs with black or brown leaf tips in late fall or early winter.

    If your shrubs are experiencing damage related to our mild fall this year, you're likely to spot these symptoms:.

    Recent findings suggest that if the damage is confined to a few leaf and needle tips, there's no need to worry: your shrub will recover, and it's a good idea to take steps to prevent further damage. If the damage is more significant, there's still a high chance of recovery but you should better protect plants from frost and have plenty of patience.

    Industry observers note that there are two primary and most likely causes of dark, dry tips on your evergreen shrubs. The distinction matters because the underlying cause determines how you help your shrub recover.

    It has been revealed that your shrubs naturally harden off for winter, a process triggered by less daylight and gradually dropping temperatures. They slow their growth and undergo some internal processes that allow them to better withstand freezing winter temperatures. To get more specific, soluble sugars begin to accumulate in the cells of leaves and needles. These sugars make it harder for water in the cells to freeze and allow the plant to better regulate water movement. As the youngest leaves go through this process, they become woodier, more mature, and more resistant to freezing injuries.

    During a mild fall, as many of us have experienced this year, some evergreens might continue producing new, soft growth instead of entering the dormancy period. This disrupts the vital process of winter hardening-off, leaving cells with high water content and underdeveloped protection. So, when temperatures finally drop, the water in cells freezes more readily. These frozen cells then rupture. Affected leaves, needles, and tips die as a result of the damage and turn brown or black.

    According to recent reports, some of the evergreens most susceptible to this type of damage include hebe, choisya, camellia, and photinia. Even plants that normally tolerate cold winters can be affected after an unusually warm fall.

    According to recent reports, desiccation or wind scorch, also known as winter burn, is another potential cause of black or brown evergreen foliage, and this can occur regardless of an unseasonable fall. Evergreen shrubs lose moisture through their leaves, even as growth slows, and cold air, winter winds and bright sun increase this moisture loss. Once the ground – and the moisture held in the soil – freezes, the shrubs’ roots can't take up water to replace what's being lost. This moisture imbalance can cause leaf and needle tissue to dry out and turn brown or black, and damage often begins at foliage tips and margins.

    In a recent development, distinguishing leaf damage caused by winter desiccation from new foliage that's died in the first cold snap is easy: if wind scorch is the issue, damage will be on the windy side of the shrub. You’ll also see that the outer leaves and needles are most affected, with the inner foliage protected. The damage from wind scorch is typically gradual rather than suddenly appearing after a frost or freeze, too.

    Sources indicate that evergreens with shallow roots like arborvitae, boxwood, rhododendron, yew, juniper and holly are particularly susceptible to winter desiccation. Any evergreen can be damaged this way, however, depending on moisture in the soil, wind levels and how protected the shrub is.

    First – and most importantly – of all, don’t rush to snip off those black tips. You can’t recover that dead tissue, and cutting it off now can cause more damage. If your shrubs are victims of the poor hardening-off that resulted from a mild fall, trimming could trigger more vulnerable growth, and also expose currently sheltered foliage to further harm. Similarly, the damage on a wind-scorched shrub will protect the foliage beneath.

    The next step depends on the cause of the leaf damage.

    Industry observers note that now you know your shrub isn’t ready for the cold, protect it from the rest of the winter weather to come. A zip-up plant jacket is an easy way to winterize shrubs that only need protecting ahead of a predicted cold snap rather than being wrapped up all winter. Another option is to wrap plants up in burlap – rolls of hessian are available from Walmart – or horticultural fleece such as this from Amazon, unwrapping plants after the cold weather has passed.

    When covering shrubs, be sure to do so loosely and use stakes inserted in the soil to hold fabric away from leaves. If your shrub is growing in a container, then wrapping the pot in bubble wrap and burlap protects roots during a prolonged freeze, too. Choose the level of protection based on your zone and how badly damaged your evergreen shrub is.

    If those dead leaf tips are caused by a wind and moisture imbalance, first check the moisture in the soil around the plants. If you're using a moisture meter, make sure it's one with a long probe like this moisture meter on Amazon so you get a reading where it matters. If the soil is dry and the ground isn’t frozen, give the root zone a good soak.

    In a recent development, next, apply a layer of mulch made from natural materials like Back to the Roots Organic Mulch, available from Amazon, around the base of each shrub. This will help conserve moisture and insulate the soil. Just be sure to keep the mulch a few inches away from the stems to prevent moisture accumulating there and causing rot or fungal disease.

    Now you need to protect your shrub from further damage from wind scorch. You could pop a frost jacket on your shrub whenever high winds are forecast, or use burlap to create a windbreak. You don’t necessarily need to cover the whole shrub; just provide a barrier from the prevailing winds. Keep checking shrubs throughout the winter, adding windbreaks and watering when the soil thaws as needed.

    These steps will help prevent more damage, but they won’t reverse the damage that has already occurred. Now, you’re probably wondering when you can remove those unsightly dead leaf tips – and you're going to have to be patient. It’s key not to prune off dead leaves or branches now as this can trigger latest growth, introduce damage or disease at the cut areas, and leave interior foliage vulnerable.

    It has been revealed that wait to prune until spring when there is no more risk of a severe frost, then use clean, sharp shears to remove dead tips. If larger areas have browned or blackened, cut these stems back to the first healthy, live bud. You can check if a branch might regrow by scraping back the outer layer with your fingernail. If it’s brown underneath, it’s dead and should be removed. If you see green, it could still sprout latest growth.

    Keep your pruning light in spring. Trim back the damaged parts and then let healthy branches and leaves grow back in before you do any heavier pruning or shaping.

    The damage for this year is done and gone, but you can learn from the incident to save your evergreen shrubs from harm next year:.

    It has been revealed that dead leaf tips on evergreen shrubs are usually a cosmetic issue, not a death sentence for your favorite plants. Follow these guidelines and your shrubs should recover, ready to shine again next year.

    Find out what's causing your precious houseplant to forgo its foliage, and whether it's a cause for concern.

    Yellowing leaves in November are usually caused by the #1 seasonal mistake houseplant parents make.

    Work out what's behind your ailing spider-plant developing brown tips in fall and nurse your houseplant back to health.

    Take these proven-to-work steps to make your yard inhospitable to snakes in fall and reduce numbers next year, too.

    End rot is a common challenge for winter squash in fall but identify the cause and it's simple to rescue the remaining crop.

    #159077. Mini Greenhouse or Cold Frame? Discover Which is Better to Protect Your Plants From Winter Weather

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1565 w)

    Mini Greenhouse or Cold Frame? Discover Which is Better to Protect Your Plants From Winter Weather

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1565 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When the forecast drops below freezing for the first time in late fall, half the neighborhood rushes out to tuck bedsheets over their mums – unless they have a greenhouse, that is.
    • It has been revealed that A mini greenhouse is a tall but narrow enclosure with wire-mesh shelves zipped inside a clear plastic cover.
    • Here's everything you need to know to make the right decision to protect your plants from frost and snow this winter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When the forecast drops below freezing for the first time in late fall, half the neighborhood rushes out to tuck bedsheets over their mums – unless they have a greenhouse, that is. But while most folk don't have the space or the budget for a full-size glasshouse, a mini greenhouse or cold frame is the affordable option to get plants through winter unscathed. But which is best when it comes to protecting plants from winter weather?

    It has been revealed that A mini greenhouse is a tall but narrow enclosure with wire-mesh shelves zipped inside a clear plastic cover. A cold frame is a low, bottomless box with a see-through lid that sits right on the dirt. Both catch sun all day, but they handle the night very differently, making the best one for you dependant on what you grow. And a Georgia winter is a very different beast from a Minnesota one, which affects how you winterize your garden in late fall.

    Here's everything you need to know to make the right decision to protect your plants from frost and snow this winter.

    In a recent development, most mini greenhouses are made from a light steel frame with two to four tiers of wire-mesh shelves. This is covered with a PVC or polyethylene cover that zips up the front, or some designs have rigid polycarbonate panels, which is why they're often referred to as 'plastic greenhouses'. To vent, you unzip and roll up the door.

    Mini greenhouses are cheap and give you a lot of growing space for a small footprint, but the plastic cover can wear out and be hard to replace, and not all products stand up to winter winds unless they're positioned in a sheltered spot. If you only use a mini greenhouse in winter, it's easy to pack up and store away for summer, or if you can remove the shelves then they're useful for growing tomatoes.

    Cold frames are typically made from wood, aluminum or brick with a hinged glass or polycarbonate lid that can be propped open on warm days. Only holding one layer of pots, a cold frame and will only fit fairly low-growing plants. They generally cost more, unless you put your DIY skills to the test and build your own cold frame, but a sturdy design with a rigid lid lasts for years. A cold frame doesn't buy you any extra growing room, however.

    Plants will usually come through a harsh 20°F (-7°C) night better in a cold frame than a mini greenhouse. Because the frame has an open base and sits directly on the ground, it benefits more from the heat of the sun. Soil soaks up the solar heat all day, which is why it's a good idea to prop the lid open a few inches on sunny days if temperatures rise above 40°F (4°C). But close the lid by late afternoon and the interior stays warm as the soil gives the heat back overnight, and the frame's solid sides slow the loss. For extra warmth, it's an easy task to bank straw or soil against the walls. too.

    So, vegetables such as lettuce, spinach, kale and other winter greens will keep growing slowly under a cold frame lid into early winter. Low perennials and young transplants often do well too, and so do plants that rot when winter rain sits on their crowns.

    Space is where a mini greenhouse wins over a cold frame. With several tiers of shelves, you can stack seedling trays, rooted cuttings and pots of hardy herbs in a space about the size of a doormat. However, a mini greenhouse sitting on paving has no soil to draw from, so it doesn't stay as warm overnight. While the interior still heats up in the day (so needs venting), thin plastic sides allow the warmth to promptly escape, so it doesn't take long for the air inside to drop to the same temperature as the air outside. A tall mini greenhouse catches every gust of wind, too, and cold air finds any gaps around zippers and seams.

    If you have a sheltered sunny wall to stand a mini greenhouse against, however, that structure will absorb the sun's heat during the day and give it back through the night, helping to stabilize temperatures. Still, don't trust thin plastic in a hard freeze – but a mini greenhouse does a great job at keeping wind and rain off hardy container plants.

    A mini greenhouse gives you extra growing space on a balcony or in a small urban garden, too.

    According to recent reports, when buying a cold frame, it's good to know that wood insulates better than metal if you live in a harsh climate. It's heavier, though, so if you want to be able to move your cold frame, then an aluminum frame also has the advantage it won't rot. Either way, look for a sturdy frame that doesn't wobble and a lid that props open at more than one height. Automatic venting is a useful upgrade if you're not at home during the day, as a temperature-activated hinge lifts the lid as the inside warms up.

    Cedar wood frame, 3.5mm polycarbonate insulation and fully opening lid with venting positions.

    Aluminum frame, 4mm polycarbonate panels and a collapsible design for easy summer storage.

    Cedar and powder-coated steel, double-wall polycarbonate lid and temperature-activated automatic lid opening.

    When buying a mini greenhouse, there's a balance to be had between budget and cover quality. A mini greenhouse with polycarbonate panels is more expensive but holds heat far better than a floppy plastic cover. If you opt for a cheaper flexible cover then look for one made of PE (polyethylene), preferably reinforced PE, rather than PVC.

    PE stays flexible in freezing temperature and copes with long-term UV exposure well. PE that's reinforced with mesh also means any rips are easily fixed, and still lets in around 85% of sunlight. PVC (polyvinyl chloride) is usually clearer so lets more light through, but tends to split and yellow over time.

    Industry observers note that look for a stiff, robust frame because a wobbly one means the cover flaps until the seams gape. It's vital that you can anchor the mini greenhouse down, too, and that the method used is suitable for the ground you plant to stand it on. Most designs will have base flaps that you can weigh down with bricks or stones, while some offer additional anchoring with ground stakes – useful if your garden is at all exposed.

    Double-layer roof design for ventilation, UV-resistant PE cover and zip-up door. Measures 50" H x 27.6" W x 19.7" D.

    Reinforced PE cover, mesh racks and 4 ropes and ground stakes. Measures 76.8" H x 57.9" W x 30.3" D.

    Sources indicate that 4mm polycarbonate panels, roof vent, sliding door and rain gutter. Measures 71.65" H x 75.98" W x 27.16" D.

    It's a simple task to upgrade a cold frame or mini greenhouse when winterizing your garden, and the cheap fixes go a long way. You could save bubble wrap to repurpose in the garden, clipping a layer inside the cover for an extra layer of trapped air. Always pick significant bubbles since they generally insulate better, like this 24-inch-wide roll of large-bubble clear wrap from Amazon. Bubble wrap does cut some light, however, and packing-grade wrap breaks down in the sun faster than horticultural film.

    On a bitter night, spreading frost cloth like this from Amazon over the plants inside also helps to insulate them, and it's easily pulled off in the morning.

    A tall mini greenhouse can tip in strong wind, and even if anchoring stakes are included, they're usually flimsy. A shed anchor kit like this from Amazon with 18-inch ground screws and steel cable will do a much better job of holding your mini greenhouse down through winter weather.

    In a recent development, if you mostly grow winter greens and low perennials, buy the cold frame since the open soil base and solid sides will give plants steadier nights. If you need plenty of space for seedlings, cuttings or taller pots, go with a mini greenhouse and expect bigger temperature swings.

    Industry observers note that whichever you pick, park it in a sunny spot out of the wind, and hang a cheap digital max/min thermometer like this from Amazon in there so you know just what degree of winter protection your plants are getting. Neither a cold frame nor a mini greenhouse will protect frost-tender plants in severe cold weather without extra insulation or a safe heat source, so bring them inside before a hard freeze. And if you do add heat, do it carefully – a soil-heating cable on a GFCI outlet turns a cold frame into a hotbed, but keep heaters away from plastic and never run a fuel-burning heater in a small closed structure.

    It has been revealed that tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success highlights that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

    #159075. Breaking: Former Garden Center Manager Reveals the Gifts Gardeners Love – and the Ones They Secretly Hate

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1886 w)

    Breaking: Former Garden Center Manager Reveals the Gifts Gardeners Love – and the Ones They Secretly Hate

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that buying a gift for the gardener on your list seems easy enough.
    • After years of working with gardeners as a garden center manager and an avid gardener myself, I can tell you the gardening gifts they really want: boots that can handle mud, pruners that cut without a fight, and tools that solve a problem, hold up over time, or make the job easier.
    • If you’re shopping for a gardener this year (or for yourself), let me share my garden center secrets to help you look past the gifts that merely look pretty in a gift bag and find the ones they’ll actually use, appreciate, and think of you every time they reach for them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that buying a gift for the gardener on your list seems easy enough. Head to the garden center, find something cutesy with flowers on it, maybe a packet of seeds, add a few assorted tools, and call it a day. They’ll appreciate the thought behind any gift, of course, but if you want to make a gardener really happy, skip the cute and go for something useful.

    After years of working with gardeners as a garden center manager and an avid gardener myself, I can tell you the gardening gifts they really want: boots that can handle mud, pruners that cut without a fight, and tools that solve a problem, hold up over time, or make the job easier. Gardening may be a hobby to some, but its actual work and the right tools make all the difference.

    If you’re shopping for a gardener this year (or for yourself), let me share my garden center secrets to help you look past the gifts that merely look pretty in a gift bag and find the ones they’ll actually use, appreciate, and think of you every time they reach for them.

    Industry observers note that the pattern may be cute, but pretty garden shoes aren’t always cut out for real gardening tasks. They may not hold up long-term and may leak.

    What gardeners actually want...

    Industry observers note that give them real gardening boots that are waterproof, durable, comfortable, and warm enough for cold weather. We want something that can handle mud, wet grass, mulch, snow, and a full day outdoors without leaving our feet wet and miserable.

    The boots from The Original Muck Boot Manufacturer check all of those boxes. Oh, and some have those cute prints, too!

    This waterproof, easy-wear chore boot is built for gardening, yard work, and everyday outdoor tasks.

    Industry observers note that gardeners do not need more tools that do just one thing. They want tools that earn their place in the shed and are useful for more than one task.

    What gardeners actually want...

    A hori hori knife is one of those tools they don’t realize how much they’ll use until they have one. It digs, weeds, cuts roots, transplants, divides plants, and tackles countless other jobs. It even has markings to help correctly plant or space seeds and bulbs. They will reach for this one over and over again.

    Features both serrated and straight edge blades, and is a fantastic gardening and landscaping tool.

    A Garden Weasel Oversized Potting Scoop, like this one from Amazon, is another multi-use tool that can be used for scooping soil, digging, planting, or even filling bird feeders with seed.

    For gardeners who love wildlife, another basic, oddly shaped container to fill with seed isn't very exciting. They want to get more out of the experience than that.

    What gardeners actually want...

    Recent findings suggest that instead, bring the birds closer with a smart feeder that captures photos and videos of their feathered visitors. They'll practically get to know their daily regulars (and probably a few squirrels, too) up close, all from their phone or tablet, rather than having to wait around by the window.

    The Kiwibit Solar Smart Bird Feeder With Camera is an upgraded, fully solar-powered model that captures 8MP photos and crisp 4K Ultra HD video, with real-time alerts when birds visit the feeder. Plus, it works with the Kiwibit app to identify more than 10,000 bird species.

    If you're on a tighter budget, then the Birdfy Bird Feeder with Camera for Beginners offers Lifetime Bird ID and 2K HD for a great price.

    The Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 works with the Kiwibit app to identify over 10,000 bird species with real-time alerts.

    Just because the package reveals a pair of pruners doesn't mean they're up to the task. Cheap pruners with dull blades can crush stems or struggle to cut even thin branches. They're frustrating for the average gardener and often end up in the trash after just a few uses.

    What gardeners actually want...

    Gift them a pair of sharp, quality bypass pruners. They don't even need to be expensive. Gardeners simply want a pair that makes clean cuts, feels comfortable in their hands, and lasts for years with just a little maintenance.

    While the F-2 pruning shears from Swiss brand Felco, available here on Amazon, are a favorite among gardeners, the affordable 5/8-inch Fiskars Bypass Pruning Shears are also well-reviewed and happen to be one of my personal favorites.

    Self-cleaning sap groove prevents sticking with a non-slip grip for cutting stems & branches.

    Speaking of maintenance, they could also benefit from a quality sharpening tool to keep not only their pruners but also their loppers and hedge clippers in good working order, such as this Corona Blade Sharpener from Amazon.

    In a recent development, if you've spent the day pruning the thick, tough stems of panicle hydrangeas, fruit trees, or thorny roses, you know how rapidly your hands can tire from the repetitive cutting. Gardeners don't need more tools that make these time-consuming jobs harder than they already are.

    What gardeners actually want...

    They want tools that save time and effort, such as cordless electric pruners, mini chainsaws, and other battery-powered garden tools that make repetitive tasks faster, easier, and less physically demanding. Many of these compact tools are small enough to fit right into a gardener's tool caddy, making them easy to carry around the yard and keep close at hand.

    These types of tools can be a real game changer, especially for gardeners who spend hours tackling demanding pruning and trimming jobs.

    Equipped with two rechargeable batteries, our cordless pruning shears provide extended runtime for continuous cutting.

    Equipped with a WORKPROX 20V 2.0Ah battery, providing up to 30 minutes of continuous runtime.

    2-in-1 functionality and a 5/16" cut capacity, making it ideal for trimming where other tools can't reach.

    It has been revealed that gardening already involves plenty of bending, kneeling, and repeatedly getting up and down, especially when it comes to weeding. While there are plenty of weeding tools on the market, many still require gardeners to spend long periods bent over or kneeling. It's no wonder backs and knees start to ache!

    What gardeners actually want...

    Give gardeners a tool that lets them work smarter, not harder. Long-handled, stand-up weed pullers help take the strain off backs and knees while making it easier to tackle weeds without constantly bending, kneeling, or getting down on the ground. Their back will thank you!

    Remove weeds without bending, pulling, or kneeling.

    Cute gloves made of thin fabric with funny sayings and colorful floral prints may look good in a gift basket, but they don't necessarily get the job done. Ill-fitting, flimsy gloves offer little protection and often end up shoved in a drawer and forgotten. On the other hand, gloves that are too bulky can make even simple gardening tasks difficult.

    What gardeners actually want...

    What gardeners really want are gloves that fit properly, offer the right protection, and are comfortable enough to wear for hours.

    Breathable gloves with a nitrile-coated palm provide excellent protection for all sorts of gardening jobs, from digging and pulling weeds to pruning roses and planting delicate seeds.

    Sources indicate that look for pairs that fit well and come in bright, easy-to-spot colors. That way, when gardeners inevitably set them down and forget where they left them, they're much easier to find!

    It has been revealed that and here's a little gift-giving tip: Buy a set of four or more! Gardeners can never have too many pairs of gloves.

    The unique form-fitting, ergonomic design fits like a second skin, allowing for unmatched precision.

    It has been revealed that gnomes, gazing balls, and flower stakes can make wonderful gifts if you know the gardener collects them. But if you're not sure, yet another garden ornament may not be the best use of your money.

    What gardeners actually want...

    Consider giving them something functional, such as a comfortable garden kneeler that flips over into a cushion-lined seat. It makes planting, working close to the ground, and tending raised beds much more comfortable. Plus, having a place to sit and take a break is always welcome after a few hours in the garden!

    Equipped with two large tool pouches, perfect for keeping your gardening tools conveniently within reach.

    According to recent reports, those little novelty herb-growing kits that use a mason jar might be cute and offer a fun way to grow something during the winter, especially when gardening with kids. However, those small containers have limited room for roots and simply won’t produce a full, lush plant. Gardeners who enjoy growing their own fresh greens and herbs are likely looking for something a little more worthwhile and practical.

    What gardeners actually want...

    According to recent reports, A good microgreens planter is a great option, allowing them to grow fresh, nutritious greens right in the kitchen or just about anywhere, regardless of the weather outside. It’s easy, practical, and provides something fresh to harvest week after week, even in the middle of winter.

    Skip the dirt and daily watering—this planter is made for simple, indoor growing.

    It has been revealed that I’ve been really enjoying my EZ Microgreens Planters from Vego Garden. I had fresh greens ready to harvest in just a little over a week, even as temperatures started dropping here in Ohio.

    I’d add in a few packets of high-quality microgreens seeds from Botanical Interests to complete this gift set.

    Small hoop houses, low tunnels, and pint-sized greenhouses can certainly be useful, but flimsy covers that don’t hold up to the wind, offer very little protection, or barely provide any room to grow can leave gardeners wanting something bigger and better.

    What gardeners actually want...

    According to recent reports, what they really want is a proper greenhouse or a well-built growing structure that can help extend the growing season, protect their plants, and give them more opportunities to grow in early spring and late fall. They want something with usable space and practical functionality, not just a flimsy cover that barely makes a difference. And if it looks gorgeous in the backyard, that's an added bonus!

    Extend your growing season for half the price of other premium greenhouses.

    For those who don't have the space or whose budget doesn't quite allow for a full-size greenhouse, a tiered, all-in-one greenhouse shelving unit, like this Home-Complete 4 Tier Mini Greenhouse with Locking Wheels and PVC Cover from Walmart, may do the trick. But let's be honest, they'll probably still be dreaming about that beautiful glass greenhouse!

    #159073. How to Prune a Christmas Tree – Fix a Too-Tall, Too-Wide, or Lopsided Tree for the Perfect Shape

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2287 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Prune a Christmas Tree – Fix a Too-Tall, Too-Wide, or Lopsided Tree for the Perfect Shape

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2287 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Unless you’re willing to settle for an artificial Christmas tree, you’re unlikely to find one that’s perfectly symmetrical.
    • It has been revealed that all of the best Christmas tree care in the world won’t help with these shaping issues.
    • Of course, knowing how to pick a Christmas tree with a good natural shape can save you some work in the first place.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Unless you’re willing to settle for an artificial Christmas tree, you’re unlikely to find one that’s perfectly symmetrical. We've all been there: you choose one that looks promising at the lot, then get it home and discover it's too tall or wide for your living room – or simply looks much more awkwardly shaped than you remembered. It’s enough to make you open the bottle of sherry you left out for Santa.

    It has been revealed that all of the best Christmas tree care in the world won’t help with these shaping issues. But a little careful pruning can make a substantial difference. Here, we will explain the steps to trim a too-tall, too-wide, or lopsided Christmas tree into a balanced, attractive centerpiece. We’ll also lay out the tools you need and the techniques you should use.

    Of course, knowing how to pick a Christmas tree with a good natural shape can save you some work in the first place. Before you begin trimming, remember that removing branches is much easier than putting them back. Work gradually, and try repositioning or fluffing branches before reaching for your pruners.

    A beautifully shaped Christmas tree should have a straight central trunk, a strong top branch to support a star or angel, and evenly spaced branches that create a full, balanced appearance.

    Sources indicate that commercial Christmas tree growers tend to encourage the classic conical Christmas tree shape through occasional pruning. They aim for a base width of around 60 to 70 percent of the tree's height, although a slimmer tree may be more practical for smaller rooms.

    Branch density matters, too. Large gaps between branch tiers can make a tree look sparse, while more closely spaced tiers create a fuller appearance – though denser branch tiers mean less space to hang ornaments.

    Recent findings suggest that the first step, once you bring the new tree into your home, is to make a fresh, straight cut about half an inch (1.3 cm) from the base of the trunk. Some sellers will do this for you before you load it into your car, but it needs to be fresh. If you're doing it yourself, a pruning saw, like Fiskars' Pro 10-Inch Pruning Saw, available on Amazon, will make the job easier. Then, put the tree straight into a sturdy container of water. This is one of the most important steps to make your Christmas tree last longer and prevent premature needle drop.

    Industry observers note that let the tree settle before doing any further trimming. Give the tree a few hours, or ideally overnight, to relax its branches. This is particularly crucial if the tree has been tightly wrapped in netting. Its branches need time to spread back into their natural positions, and what initially looks like an awkward gap or uneven section may become much less noticeable.

    Sources indicate that once the branches have relaxed, walk around the tree and look at it from several angles. Identify any protruding branches, bare patches, or uneven growth before deciding what actually needs cutting.

    You’ll need clean, sharp tools to prune a real Christmas tree into a pleasing cone shape. With the right tools and techniques, you can create a full, appealing tree no matter how tall, wide, or wonky it started out.

    You can buy a hundred different tools for pruning trees, but you really don’t need more than a handful to prune a real Christmas tree. For smaller branches, a pair of budget-friendly pruners, like Fiskars Bypass Pruning Shears, will give you the control needed to make clean, precise cuts. For thicker branches, use loppers, like Corona ComfortGEL Bypass Loppers, which provide extra cutting power.

    For cutting through the trunk, use a sharp pruning saw or handsaw. Make sure the cut is straight so the tree sits securely in its stand.

    Sources indicate that is your Christmas tree too tall for your space? That’s usually one of the easiest Christmas tree problems to deal with, so don’t fret. First, measure your ceiling height, then subtract the height you need for the tree stand and tree topper, plus at least 1–2 inches (2.5–5 cm) of clearance. This is the perfect height for your new tree. Then measure the tree to see how much you need to remove.

    Recent findings suggest that if you only need a modest reduction (say, a few inches), cut the excess length from the bottom of the trunk. Just make sure enough bare trunk remains to fit securely into the stand without forcing the lower branches against its rim. Then put the tree into its stand – ideally one with a built-in water reservoir, like the Krinner Genie Christmas Tree Stand.

    Recent findings suggest that if your tree is significantly too tall, removing a large section of the trunk could also mean losing its attractive lower branches. In this case, you may need to shorten the central leader at the top instead. This is the upright shoot that forms the tree's tip.

    Sometimes the leader is disproportionately tall and can easily be shortened without spoiling the tree's shape. Other times, cutting off the original tip can ruin its natural outline and remove the little knobbly buds and side shoots that help hold a tree topper in place. Indeed, it might be better to go without a topper rather than making a drastic cut. So treat trimming the tip of your Christmas tree as a last resort, and only if you think it will work with its natural shape.

    If you do decide to take this step, trim the leader carefully to the desired height. Then assess the tree's newly introduced shape and, if necessary, selectively shorten the surrounding branches until you achieve a symmetrical, conical outline. Work gradually, stepping back regularly to check your progress.

    When a tree is too wide to fit gracefully in your home, you can trim its branches. A traditionally shaped Christmas tree has a base width of around two-thirds its height. But it’s a good idea to measure the floor space where the tree will stand to make sure that the “ideal” shape will work for you.

    Sources indicate that start by positioning the tree where you want it to stand and turning it to find the most attractive side. If branches at the back prevent it from fitting neatly against the wall, trim these first. Then, look at the tree from the front and sides, shortening any branches that stick out too far or spoil its overall shape.

    Work gradually, removing a little at a time, and step back often to check the results. You don't need to trim every branch to the same length – the aim is to create a balanced, natural-looking tree that fits comfortably in its space.

    Recent findings suggest that for branches that genuinely need shortening, make cuts within the green, needle-covered portion of the growth. Avoid cutting too deeply into the bare, woody sections, as this can leave obvious gaps in the foliage that won't fill out.

    Remember that different types of Christmas trees naturally have different shapes. Some firs have a dense, compact outline, while certain spruces and pines have more open branching. Work with the tree's natural form rather than trying to force every variety into exactly the same silhouette.

    It has been revealed that it’s easier to talk about a too-tall or too-wide Christmas tree than one that’s just kind of weird. Whether it's lopsided or just plain wonky, you can still improve that uneven Christmas tree shape to make it presentable.

    Recent findings suggest that first, check that the trunk is standing straight in its base. Sometimes a tree that looks lopsided simply needs adjusting in the stand rather than pruning.

    To shape a lopsided Christmas tree, keep a cone shape in the front of your mind. Prune the upper branches shorter than the lower ones, and remember that the base width should be about two-thirds the tree's height. To achieve these goals, keep stepping back to see how things look.

    In a recent development, take off any dead or damaged branches, then clip back any that protrude too far and spoil the tree's outline. If one side is particularly dense, you can selectively shorten a few branches to create a more balanced appearance. Work gradually, as it's easy to remove too much.

    Industry observers note that some unevenness comes from the way the tree grew. Christmas trees produce successive tiers of branches as they develop, and the amount of growth between these tiers influences how dense or open the finished tree appears. If one section has widely spaced branches, pruning alone won't necessarily make it look fuller.

    Start by fluffing nearby branches or gently repositioning longer ones to disguise any gaps. You can also fold flexible branches into place and secure them with twine. If one side is woefully sparse, turn the tree so that this side is against the wall.

    Recent findings suggest that alternatively, you can borrow a branch from a particularly dense area of the tree and use it to fill an obvious gap. Simply cut the branch and secure it to the trunk or a sturdy neighboring branch with green wire, like this Pauleen floral wire from Amazon, positioning it to blend in with the surrounding foliage. Make sure it's firmly attached before adding any decorations.

    It has been revealed that if you'd rather not cut branches from elsewhere on your tree, artificial Christmas tree filler branches or greenery picks can work just as well. Look for ones that closely match the color and texture of your tree's needles, like these Hananona faux pine branches, and tuck them into sparse areas to create a fuller, more balanced appearance.

    In a recent development, you may also be able to disguise a sparse section by trimming back some of the heavier surrounding growth, helping the branches appear more evenly distributed. However, avoid cutting away too much greenery in an attempt to fill a gap – you could end up creating another one.

    According to recent reports, the only time you have to worry about a tree’s health is when it is alive. If you have a cut Christmas tree, it is no longer growing. That means that you do not have to worry about its health. Instead, trim the tree to fit well and look nice in your home.

    Sources indicate that however, excessive Christmas tree shearing can still affect its appearance and stability. Removing too many lower branches may leave the trunk exposed, while cutting away large sections of the crown can make it difficult to achieve a natural shape.

    If, however, you buy a living Christmas tree you wish to plant, you do have to worry about keeping the tree healthy. Over-trimming can send the tree into shock or even kill it. The general rule is never to take off more than a quarter of the foliage annually. For most trimmings, stick to 10 percent.

    Don't cut conifers back to the woody inner branches. Most will not sprout new needles from these branches. Limit your pruning to green, needle-bearing growth. The only exception is if you remove an entire branch back to the trunk.

    Recent findings suggest that if you're growing your own Christmas tree in the garden or keeping a living tree to use again in future years, pruning requires a different approach. Unlike a cut tree, a living evergreen needs to maintain healthy growth and develop a strong, balanced structure.

    It has been revealed that young Christmas trees generally need only light corrective pruning during their first few years. This might involve removing damaged branches, correcting an uneven shape, or dealing with two competing upright shoots. Ideally, the tree should have one dominant central leader to maintain a straight trunk and a natural pointed crown.

    More regular shaping can begin as the tree becomes established, often around its third growing season. For many Christmas tree species, growers carry out their main shearing once the fresh shoots have finished extending but before the fresh growth becomes fully firm. The timing varies according to the species and growing conditions.

    Industry observers note that for a living Christmas tree you hope to keep for years, though, it's best to prune conservatively. Focus on correcting problems rather than heavily shearing the entire tree, and always check the pruning requirements of the particular species you're growing.

    Many people get overexcited when they start pruning a Christmas tree and are shocked to find out they have cut off too much. If this is you, take a breath. It’s only a Christmas tree. Resist the temptation to keep cutting elsewhere to even things up. A few strategically placed decorations will usually disguise the problem more effectively than further pruning.

    If you have snipped a few times too many and created a bare spot (or two!), here are a few tips for covering up the damage:.

    As you move through the necessary pruning, you’ll want to keep these few key rules in mind:.

    #159072. Want To Befriend A Woodpecker? Here Are 6 Easy Ways To Attract These Striking Birds To Your Yard

    Want To Befriend A Woodpecker? Here Are 6 Easy Ways To Attract These Striking Birds To Your Yard

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (964 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Long tied to forest and earth deities, woodpeckers are some of the most fascinating (and symbolically-laden) birds to welcome into your backyard.
    • According to recent reports, that's right, folks; the birth month bird for August babies everywhere, the woodpecker represents curiosity, persistence, and determination.
    • In a recent development, whether you believe in that or not, though, there's no denying that woodpeckers are considered one of the world's most popular birds for a reason...
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Long tied to forest and earth deities, woodpeckers are some of the most fascinating (and symbolically-laden) birds to welcome into your backyard.

    According to recent reports, that's right, folks; the birth month bird for August babies everywhere, the woodpecker represents curiosity, persistence, and determination. (And don't even get us started on what it means if they're the first bird you spot on January 1st!).

    In a recent development, whether you believe in that or not, though, there's no denying that woodpeckers are considered one of the world's most popular birds for a reason... so, yes, it makes sense you'd like to befriend one!

    Oh sure, they might seem like woodland-only visitors, but there are actually several things you can do to encourage woodpeckers into your yard. In fact, whether you're hoping to spot a great spotted woodpecker, downy woodpecker, or another local species, a few simple changes can make your outdoor space a more welcoming place.

    Sources indicate that suet is one of the easiest foods to use to attract woodpeckers, especially during colder months when birds need extra energy and natural food sources become harder to find. Make sure, though, that you use a sturdy suet feeder designed to allow clinging birds to feed comfortably, and position it somewhere quiet where birds feel safe.

    It has been revealed that you should also take care to choose quality suet cakes (you want the kind with seeds or nuts in!) and keep feeders clean. It may take a wee bit of time and patience for woodpeckers to discover your new offering, but once they find a reliable food source, they may return regularly.

    Suet isn't the only food worth serving, as woodpeckers also enjoy peanuts and sunflower seeds, particularly black oil sunflower seeds, so long as you pop them in the sort of feeders that allow woodpeckers to perch or cling while feeding. (They don't like it one bit when you scatter food across the ground).

    As ever, we must stress that you should never offer salted or flavored nuts to wildlife.

    It's all well and good teasing them in, but if you want woodpeckers to stick around, you need to think beyond feeders. And the best way to do this? By planting trees that provide insects, places to forage and shelter in abundance, of course!

    In a recent development, take care to choose a tree that suits your available space and growing conditions, and remember that even a young tree can contribute to a more wildlife-friendly garden over time. Something like an oak is an excellent long-term habitat investment, while a birch offers lots of opportunities for birds to search for insects.

    Sources indicate that A smaller ornamental tree that offers spring flowers, berries for birds, and beautiful fall color is also a good option for gardens with less room. Something like a serviceberry could work really well!

    Shop Woodpecker-Friendly Trees:.

    Recent findings suggest that I've noted it before and I'll say it again, but a perfectly tidy garden isn't necessarily the most wildlife-friendly one. Dead branches, logs and tree stumps might not be the prettiest to look at (although that's changing; they've been stealing the spotlight at the RHS Chelsea Flower Show across the pond for years) but they can provide valuable habitat for insects and other invertebrates that woodpeckers forage for.

    Industry observers note that if you have a dead tree or limb that can safely remain, then, consider leaving it in place rather than removing it automatically. You could also create a small log pile or stumpery in a quiet corner of your yard. As the wood decays, it can add visual interest and become a bug buffet for woodpeckers and other birds.

    If you'd love to attract green woodpeckers in particular, consider giving your lawn a little more freedom, as these birds are particularly fond of ants ; in fact, they love nothing more than to use their long tongues to dig into nests and crevices to sccop them out and gobble them up.

    According to recent reports, avoid pesticides, then, and leave a patch of grass to grow longe if you can. You don't need to abandon lawn care completely, but creating a less manicured patch? It will encourage much more natural wildlife activity.

    Just like other backyard birds, woodpeckers need fresh water for drinking and bathing. A shallow birdbath with gently sloping sides is a must, then, especially during hot weather or when natural water sources freeze.

    Sources indicate that be sure to pop it somewhere relatively quiet, with nearby trees or shrubs where birds can retreat if startled, but without dense cover immediately beside it where predators might lurk. A fine balance to strike, but a vital one, as I'm sure you'll agree.

    It has been revealed that look, attracting woodpeckers isn't about transforming your yard overnight. By providing reliable food, planting trees, preserving natural habitat and offering fresh water, though, you can make your outdoor space a place where wildlife feels welcome. And when that distinctive drumming or flash of color finally catches your eye? Well, then you'll know the effort was all worth it.

She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

    #159071. 7 Popular Garden Plants That Need Extra TLC Before Winter – Here's How to Protect Them From the Cold

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1460 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    7 Popular Garden Plants That Need Extra TLC Before Winter – Here's How to Protect Them From the Cold

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1460 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With winter just around the corner, your garden is busy adjusting to the changes in light and temperature and, while some plants won’t fail to return next year, others are more vulnerable and need your help to survive.
    • It has been revealed that some of these garden stalwarts are tender perennials that simply won't survive outdoors in winter, while others are technically hardy but still a little vulnerable, so overwintering these plants well is vital.
    • Sources indicate that dahlias are some of the most varied and prized flowers of a late summer and fall garden, but they’re really only hardy in zones 8 through 11.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With winter just around the corner, your garden is busy adjusting to the changes in light and temperature and, while some plants won’t fail to return next year, others are more vulnerable and need your help to survive. Many of our favorite flowering plants are the most susceptible to harm from changing temperatures, deep freezes and drying winter winds, so if you want lots of blooms again next year, give them the winter protection they need.

    It has been revealed that some of these garden stalwarts are tender perennials that simply won't survive outdoors in winter, while others are technically hardy but still a little vulnerable, so overwintering these plants well is vital. From protecting shrubs growing in the ground to digging bulbs up to take indoors, here's how to protect plants through winter so they wake up healthy in spring, ready for another bumper season of blooms.

    Sources indicate that dahlias are some of the most varied and prized flowers of a late summer and fall garden, but they’re really only hardy in zones 8 through 11. Their tuberous roots are susceptible to getting mushy in wet conditions and frozen in cold winter ground so leaving them in the ground is risky, especially in zones 6 and colder.

    The best way to protect these plants for flowers next year is to lift dahlia tubers out of the ground after the first deep frost blackens the foliage. Cut the stems back to a couple inches, then carefully dig around and lift out the crown and tubers. Let these dry for a few days to cure and then store dahlia tubers in a box of wood shavings – a compressed bale of natural pet bedding such as this from Amazon is a cheap and convenient way to buy. Keep the box in a cool but frost-free, dry storage area such as an unheated garage, and you'll overwinter dahlias to replant next spring.

    Another plant that benefits from lifting is canna, which is only generally hardy in zones 7 through 10 because it grows from rhizomes that are vulnerable in freezing winter ground. Exact hardiness depends on the variety, so know your type and growing zone.

    It has been revealed that once the foliage has blackened after a frost, cut the stems back to four to six inches (10 to 15 cm) and then carefully dig up canna rhizomes to store for the winter. As with dahlias, it’s best to let these dry for a few days before storing them in a material like wood shavings. Overwinter canna rhizomes in a dark, cool and dry storage area until spring weather has warmed up enough to replant them outdoors.

    According to recent reports, one of the most popular hydrangeas for its bright blue or pink flowers, bigleaf hydrangeas, also known as mophead hydrangeas, are typically hardy in zones 5 through 9. However, while the shrubs themselves cope with cold weather just fine, the matter with overwintering hydrangea shrubs that flower on old wood is the potential damage to next year’s flower buds that have developed before winter arrives. A cold snap can damage these buds, reducing the number of flowers you get next summer.

    Sources indicate that to protect hydrangea buds, you’ll need to do more than simply covering the roots zone with mulch. Place four stakes in a square around the shrub and wrap burlap like this from Walmart for protection. In a very cold climate, increase the insulation by filling the space between the burlap and the plant with dry leaves.

    Recent findings suggest that hybrid tea roses can be hardy from zones 4 through 9, but there is some variation by cultivar, and they're still a little vulnerable to cold weather compared to other types of roses. So, to overwinter roses in a region with a harsh climate, give them some winter protection to ensure they make it through to spring in a healthy state, ready for strong growth.

    Your roses are vulnerable to damage caused by freeze-thaw cycles in the soil and winter damage to canes. First, clean up any plant debris on the ground to reduce the risk of disease, then loosely tie the canes together for extra support in damaging winter winds. Mound soil or compost around the base of the plant and for a final layer of insulation, top with a natural mulch such as Miracle-Gro All Natural Mulch, available from The Home Depot.

    Industry observers note that rosemary is a Mediterranean herb that's generally hardy in zones 8 through 10. The best way to overwinter rosemary in colder climates is to bring it inside: trying to protect this plant outside with mulch is risky as it's very susceptible to wet, cold soil and drying winter winds. However, using a mulch is helpful in zones 7 or 8 to give the roots a little extra insulation.

    Industry observers note that in colder areas, dig up your rosemary plant and move it into a pot that you can bring it indoors. Even better, grow rosemary in a pot year-round as it won’t appreciate being dug out of the ground once established. This Mediterranean herb is one of those plants that grow better in terracotta pots because of the well-drained conditions the porous clay walls create. And because the pot won't be left outside in freezing temperatures, a cheap terracotta planter like this from Lowe's is all you need.

    Rosemary doesn't tolerate soggy roots so to improve drainage, mix perlite like Back to the Roots Organic Perlite, available from Walmart, into any all-purpose potting mix at a ratio of 1:3. Indoors, give your potted plant a cool, bright spot and avoid overwatering.

    Species and varieties of Colocasia and Alocasia offer large, striking, tropical leaves in summer but are only hardy in zones 8 through 11. Elephant ears grow from corms (large underground structures similar to tubers) which should be dug up for winter in colder growing zones.

    Recent findings suggest that to store Elephant ear corms over winter, let the foliage die back after a frost, then cut back the stems and leaves. Dig around the corm and lift it from the ground, allowing it to dry for up to two weeks before storing in wood shavings in a cool, dry spot. If your Elephant ear is growing in a pot, and small enough, the other option is bring it indoors for winter. While some types can be kept actively growing to enjoy as a houseplant, it's more usual to trim and overwinter tropical plants indoors in a semi-dormant state in a bright but cool spot.

    Industry observers note that many salvias are winter hardy up to zone 3, but in regions with cold winters, more tender varieties are usually grown as annuals. Alternatively, you can try to protect these tender salvia varieties like Brazilian sage or gentian sage from winter weather, and this strategy works best in borderline zones like 6 or 7.

    To overwinter tender salvias outside, use a thick layer of an airy natural mulch such as long-needle pine straw mulch like this from Amazon around the root zone and crown. In a more exposed garden, bark chips like these Pine Mulch Nuggets, also from Amazon, are heavier but create the same airy conditions. Leave the stems in place as they're hollow and trap air that can help insulate the crown.

    If you're growing tender salvias in containers, simply bring them inside for the winter, placing them in a spot with bright light and reduce watering as growth will slow.

    In a recent development, timing for winter protection depends on the plant and your local climate and weather in your USDA zone. Tender plants should be brought inside before the first frost, but for plants that grow from tubers, rhizomes or corms that need lifting from the ground, wait until after the first deep frost.

    Sources indicate that for mostly hardy perennials that simply need a little protection to remain healthy outside, you need to strike a balance between acting before the ground freezes and waiting until the plant goes dormant. Insulating these plants from the cold by mulching or covering too early can delay dormancy and encourage growth that's quickly damaged once temperatures drop.

    Protecting your precious plants before winter arrives isn't complicated or difficult. You simply need to know what you're growing and how the plants tolerate your local winters, then protect them accordingly. A little effort now will reward you next year with strong fresh growth as soon as temperatures rise in spring, and an abundant display of flowers.

    Industry observers note that mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.
