    Industry observers note that if you love home cooking, then what could be more appealing than picking fresh herbs and lettuce leaves – or even flavorful cherry tomatoes or chilis – right from your kitchen countertop? The best indoor garden systems let you grow your own organic produce year-round, even when it’s freezing outside. And unlike a backyard veggie garden, they take up hardly any space: just a small corner near a free power outlet.

    Recent findings suggest that offering features like built-in grow lights, automated watering, and often hydroponic setups, indoor growing systems make it easy to produce fast and surprisingly substantial harvests. Prices, features, and growing capabilities vary considerably, but most systems are straightforward to use and designed with beginners in mind. Some models have a small footprint, while others offer more capacity for bigger harvests.

    With so many systems to choose from, finding the right one for your needs can be confusing. The Gardening Know How team has tested some of the leading models and shares firsthand experiences with setup, growing performance, maintenance, and harvesting in this guide. We will help you compare the models, identify the features that matter most, and choose the best system for your space, budget, and growing ambitions.

    Here we round up three of the best indoor garden systems. Scroll down to read more detailed reviews from testing each product hands-on. You can also use the links to jump to the indoor garden that interests you the most.

    Sources indicate that if you're new to indoor growing, the Click & Grow Smart Garden 9 is an easy way to get started, ideal for fresh herbs, salad greens, and even dwarf tomatoes. With automatic lighting and self-watering capability, it uses pre-seeded pods, making it easy to get started and delivering great results. Just bear in mind that the replacement seed pods add to the ongoing cost.

    The Auk Mini combines a compact footprint with a stylish Scandinavian-inspired design, making it ideal for smaller kitchens (especially if you're fond of the IKEA aesthetic). It's exceptionally easy to use, and you can grow your own choice of seeds without buying special pods. With room for just four plants, though, it's better for fresh herbs as opposed to more substantial harvests.

    Industry observers note that if you love the idea of enhancing your growing with the latest tech, then the LetPot LPH-Max is the indoor garden for you. This impressive hydroponic system fits a variety of herbs, greens, and vegetables. Its advanced smart features offer plenty of control, but setup can be fiddly for some consumers, and some automated functions require extra equipment.

    Drawing on our extensive gardening experience, we evaluated each system for ease of setup and use, build quality, efficiency, crop performance, and overall value for money. Each reviewer tested their indoor garden for at least eight weeks in their own kitchen, assessing everything from initial setup to ongoing maintenance and harvesting. As the systems were tested by different experts in their own homes, growing conditions varied slightly, but all reviewers followed the same assessment criteria.

    From stylish, compact designs to more advanced hydroponic systems, here's how they performed in our kitchens – and who we'd recommend them for.

    It has been revealed that after four months of testing the Click & Grow Smart Garden 9, I can honestly say it's so low-maintenance it feels illegal. Setup took about 10 minutes, including time to read the instructions. Growing tomatoes, lettuce, herbs, and flowers is as easy as loading a coffee pod into a capsule machine: just pop the pre-seeded pods into the reusable grow cups and click them into place. It's completely mess-free, and the built-in grow light means you don't need a sunny windowsill.

    Industry observers note that watering is just as easy. I refill the reservoir about once a week, and the system handles the rest. A handy water-level indicator takes away the guesswork. I even went out of town for two weeks, and my plants kept growing without any care.

    I grew basil, lettuce, dwarf tomatoes, and marjoram. The lettuce grew quickly and made delicious summer salads, and the basil brought wonderful flavor to my Italian dishes. I was most impressed, though, by the cherry tomatoes. I transplanted a few spare seedlings into standard pots under grow lights, but the Smart Garden tomatoes grew much larger and produced fruit about two months earlier.

    The only disappointment was the marjoram. It sprouted well but barely grew, possibly because the larger basil and tomato plants blocked its light.

    It has been revealed that overall, the Smart Garden 9 has been a really fun, easy, and delicious project. Its sleek design looks great in my kitchen, and I'd highly recommend it to beginners or experienced gardeners looking for a hassle-free way to grow fresh produce year-round.

    In a recent development, reviewed by Kathleen Walters. Read the full review for more details.

    Recent findings suggest that the Auk Mini is easily one of the most stylish indoor growing systems I've come across. With its sleek Scandinavian design featuring wooden supports and a choice of black or white finishes, it's a world away from the more clinical-looking hydroponic systems on the market. You can also choose from three base finishes – cork, oak, or walnut – so it's easy to find one that looks at home in your kitchen.

    Recent findings suggest that setting it up couldn't have been simpler. I just pushed the wooden supports into either side of the base, threaded through the power cable, and attached the adjustable grow light on top. Then it was a case of filling each of the four mini planters with the supplied coco coir and planting the seeds. Mine came with basil and parsley, so I was ready to start growing straight away. Adding the coir was a little messy, and there aren't any convenient pre-seeded pods like you get with some other systems. However, the massive advantage is that you can use whatever seeds you like (within reason), rather than being tied to a brand's refills.

    Sources indicate that the water reservoir has an indicator that tells you when it's full or needs refilling, and you also get two little bottles of nutrients labeled Grow and Flavor – which felt delightfully Alice in Wonderland! You just pump these into the reservoir as directed. The grow light has different settings and a timer, and I particularly liked being able to position it low over the seedlings, then raise it as the herbs grew taller.

    Sources indicate that within six to seven weeks, I was harvesting fresh herbs, which was very pleasing. I also loved how neat and self-contained the whole system was once it was set up. It's attractive enough to leave out on display rather than hide away in a utility room, and it has taken pride of place on my kitchen countertop.

    According to recent reports, the main limitation is its size. With room for just four plants, it's really designed for growing a few fresh herbs rather than producing substantial harvests. But if you want something compact, easy to use, and great-looking, then the Auk Mini is a lovely choice. There's now a newer Mini 2, but the original Mini is still available while stocks last.

    Sources indicate that the LetPot LPH-Max makes it easy to grow plenty of edible plants indoors year-round. With 21 small pods and an alternative tray for two larger plants, you can grow practically a whole garden right in your kitchen. It's mess-free, too – no dirt required. Just fill the tank with water, add plant food, and sow your seeds in the sponge-like pods.

    The system was pretty easy to set up, though it took me about an hour to read the directions and work out how everything fit together. I was genuinely shocked by how well my basil grew in just water and plant food. Hydroponics is kind of amazing!

    However, I did run into a few frustrations. I wanted to try the automatic watering and feeding, but it requires an extra 7-liter reservoir to refill the tank. With a rambunctious cat, limited space, and newly refinished hardwood floors, that wasn't practical, so I used manual mode instead. The top tray didn't fit properly, and I was also disappointed that seeds weren't included.

    Sources indicate that ultimately, I think the LetPot LPH-Max is a good choice for those with hydroponics experience or who enjoy integrating technology into gardening. The app provides helpful growing information and remote controls, though a few features didn't work as expected. For beginners or anyone short on space, I'd recommend starting with a simpler system.

    Sources indicate that reviewed by Laura Walters. Read the full review for more details.

    The AeroGarden Harvest is a compact, beginner-friendly hydroponic system that grows up to six herbs, vegetables, or flowers, with a 20W LED grow light, automatic lighting, and handy reminders for adding water and nutrients.

    The Ahopegarden Hydroponic Growing System has a double-layer design that offers a space-efficient alternative to other countertop gardens, with space for 44 pods.

    The iDOO Hydroponic Growing System packs plenty of features into an affordable countertop garden, including Wi-Fi app control, adjustable LED grow lights, automatic timers, and a built-in fan and water pump, with space to grow up to 12 plants.

    Indoor garden systems can make it easy to grow fresh herbs, salad greens, and even vegetables, but there's quite a difference between compact countertop systems and larger, fully automated hydroponic systems. Before buying, think about what you want to grow, how much space you have, and how much time you're willing to spend looking after your plants. These are the main things to consider.

    Start by deciding where to position your indoor garden. Countertop systems are ideal for kitchens, but check the dimensions carefully – including the grow light's maximum height. These are often height-adjustable, but not always. You'll need enough clearance for plants to grow, as well as easy access to refill the water reservoir and harvest your crops.

    Sources indicate that plant capacity is another notable consideration. Smaller systems, such as the four-pot Auk Mini, are ideal for keeping a few fresh herbs on hand, while larger models can grow a wider variety of crops. However, just because an indoor garden has 20 growing positions doesn't mean you can actually grow 20 mature tomato plants. Larger crops like tomatoes need more room for their roots and foliage, so you may need to leave some planting spaces empty. But you can plant several herbs and lettuces as cut-and-come-again crops.

    It has been revealed that indoor garden systems are mainly used for herbs and leafy greens, including basil, parsley, lettuce, and arugula. These grow relatively quickly, don't need much space, and can provide repeat harvests.

    However, if you're hoping to grow tomatoes, peppers, or strawberries, you'll need to be more selective. Fruiting crops generally need more lighting, more growing space, and a longer growing period. Look for a system with an adjustable grow light and enough height to accommodate mature plants. Compact or dwarf varieties are usually the best choice.

    Industry observers note that many indoor garden systems use hydroponics, meaning plants grow without traditional soil. Instead, their roots receive water with nutrients added using liquid feed, and they are often supported by sponges or another growing medium. These systems can be very efficient, but you'll need to keep the water reservoir topped up and add nutrients regularly.

    It has been revealed that other systems use specially formulated growing media, such as Click & Grow's pre-seeded Smart Soil pods or the coco coir supplied with the Auk Mini. These can be particularly straightforward for beginners.

    It's also worth checking whether you're restricted to the manufacturer's own seed pods. Some systems require you to buy compatible refills, while others allow you to use your own seeds, giving you more freedom to experiment with different varieties and potentially saving money over time.

    One of the biggest advantages of an indoor garden system is that you don't need a sunny windowsill. Built-in LED grow lights provide all the light the plants need, and most systems include a timer to switch them on and off automatically.

    According to recent reports, look for adjustable light height, particularly if you want to grow anything taller than herbs or lettuce. Some systems also offer different lighting modes for leafy growth and flowering or fruiting crops.

    Sources indicate that more advanced models include touchscreen controls, smartphone apps, automatic nutrient dosing, and water-level alerts. These features can be convenient, but they aren't essential for successful growing. A simpler system with reliable lighting and watering is often a better choice if you're new to indoor gardening.

    Sources indicate that although indoor garden systems are low-maintenance, they aren't completely hands-off. You will still need to refill the water reservoir, add liquid fertilizer where required, prune plants, and harvest regularly. Hydroponic systems may also need periodic cleaning to prevent algae buildup and keep pumps and water lines working properly.

    Consider how easy the reservoir is to access and clean, whether the system has a water-level indicator, and how often you'll need to refill it. If you travel frequently, a larger reservoir or automatic watering feature could be particularly useful.

    It has been revealed that indoor garden systems range range from fairly affordable countertop models to high-tech setups costing several hundred dollars or more. However, the initial purchase price isn't the only expense to consider.

    Recent findings suggest that LED grow lights use electricity, although they're generally more energy-efficient than older lighting technologies. You can check the wattage and daily operating time to estimate running costs.

    You'll also need to factor in the cost of replacement seed pods, the growing media, nutrients, and potentially other accessories. Proprietary pods can make planting wonderfully convenient, but the costs can add up if you're growing continuously.

    According to recent reports, finally, think about what you actually want from your indoor garden. If your main goal is to save money on groceries, a small system growing a handful of herbs may take a long time to pay for itself. But if you enjoy gardening, want fresh ingredients year-round, or simply love watching things grow, the convenience and enjoyment can make it a worthwhile investment.

    Sources indicate that yes. Indoor garden systems can be a worthwhile investment if you enjoy growing your own food and want a to be harvesting fresh herbs and leaves throughout the year. They're particularly useful if you don't have a garden or want to keep growing through winter. However, they're unlikely to save you a fortune on groceries, especially once you factor in electricity, nutrients, and replacement growing supplies. The real value lies in the convenience, enjoyment, and satisfaction of harvesting your own produce whenever you need it.

    Recent findings suggest that indoor garden systems are ideal for growing herbs such as basil, parsley, cilantro, mint, and chives, along with leafy greens like lettuce, arugula, spinach, and kale. Some systems can also be used to grow smaller vegetables, including dwarf tomatoes, peppers, and even strawberries. The key is choosing plants that suit the available growing space and lighting. Fast-growing, compact crops tend to give the best results.

    Industry observers note that most small indoor garden systems are inexpensive to run, thanks to energy-efficient LED grow lights. For example, a 20-watt light running for 16 hours a day uses approximately 9.6 kWh of electricity per month. At an electricity rate of $0.17 per kWh, that works out to around $1.63 a month. Larger systems with more powerful lighting, pumps, and automated features will use more electricity.

    In a recent development, yes, but you'll need the right system and varieties. Compact or dwarf tomatoes are particularly well suited to indoor growing, provided they receive enough light and have room to develop. Strawberries can also grow successfully indoors, although they need sufficient light, nutrients, and pollination to produce fruit. Look for a system with adjustable lighting and enough space for mature plants, and avoid overcrowding.

    It has been revealed that yes. Because hydroponic plants grow without traditional soil, they rely on nutrients dissolved in the water to provide the minerals they need. Most systems come with a starter supply of specially formulated liquid nutrients. Avoid using ordinary garden fertilizer unless the manufacturer specifically recommends it, as it may not contain the right balance of nutrients or dissolve properly. Some systems automate nutrient dosing, while others require you to add it manually.

    In a recent development, absolutely. In fact, many indoor garden systems are designed specifically for people with little or no gardening experience. Models with pre-seeded pods, automatic grow lights, and self-watering reservoirs take much of the guesswork out of growing plants. The Click & Grow Smart Garden 9 is a particularly beginner-friendly option, while systems such as the Auk Mini offer more flexibility to experiment with your own seeds. Start with easy crops like basil or lettuce, follow the instructions, and you'll soon be enjoying your first homegrown harvest.

    Industry observers note that melanie is an experienced gardener and has worked in homes and gardens media for over 20 years. She previously served as Editor on Period Living magazine, and worked for Homes & Gardens, Gardening Etc, Real Homes, and Homebuilding & Renovating. Melanie has spent the last few years transforming her own garden, which is constantly evolving as a work in progress. She is also a passionate organic home grower, having experimented with almost every type of vegetable at some point. In her home, Melanie tends to an extensive houseplant collection and is particularly fond of orchids.

    #159069. How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1032 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finegardening ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, people often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a initiative.
    • I like to create purpose-driven designs.
    • Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, people often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a initiative. While every client and garden is different, I usually start with the same basic questions.

    I like to create purpose-driven designs. For example, I’m often called on to solve a problem, even if it is simply “I have a newly introduced house and a blank slate.” It may be just a section of the garden, the front yard, or something specific like repairing a garden after a new septic system installation or after a new house is built next door.

    Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light. Questions help people consider things they would not normally think about. As a result, these conversations define their needs and desires, helping me combine different elements into a cohesive design.

    The same approach applies to projects in my own garden. I don’t give myself a questionnaire, but I do ask myself the same questions. First, I assess the challenges, the location of the area in relation to the rest of the property, and the environmental conditions that will influence the planting.

    In a new garden, the major goal is often screening. Most people want privacy to live their lives outside without having to see a neighboring house, road, commercial area, or vacant lot.

    Privacy was one of the major considerations when planning my grass garden. There was no privacy between my property and the neighboring property. I could see my neighbors eat their dinner, watch them play with their grandchildren, and even see them argue. Their house was also too close to the property line, and in fact, their sidewalk was on my property. That was a problem.

    Because the sidewalk was already there when I moved in, I had to incorporate it into my design, but I could still make it disappear visually.

    It has been revealed that I started out with some tall elements at the back of the bed to start the screening process. I positioned these plants so I could maintain them from my property without having branches extend over the property line. Keeping their mature size in mind also helped avoid potential conflicts with the neighboring property. Soft screens made of trees and tall shrubs (both evergreen and deciduous) offer privacy without creating a harsh, artificial boundary line.

    Read More: 20 Unique Hedging Plant Options.

    Looking at the space, I could see a definite focal point within my property. With the neighbor behind me, the view naturally led the eye toward the water. Therefore, I designed a one-sided border rather than an island bed meant to be viewed from multiple directions. Making the border as deep as 20 feet in places gave me enough room to continue screening the neighboring property while also providing some sound buffering.

    Recent findings suggest that understanding the environmental conditions was the next step. The back edge is on the north side of my property. The large trees and shrubs would not shade the rest of the bed. This meant the bed would be in full sun all day, all season long.

    It has been revealed that what a challenge for this PNW native who grew up mostly in the forest (or woods, as we called it). I had to learn about plants that liked full sun, drying winds, and dry soil so they could thrive. Rather than trying to re-create the shaded woodland conditions I knew best, I needed to work with what the site naturally offered.

    Read More: Summer-Dry Gardening: A Visit to Beth Chatto’s Gravel Garden.

    Growing up in the forest, I longed for wide-open sky and long views. Above all, I wanted to immerse myself in the garden. A long row of hedging plants that I could only look at wasn’t what I had in mind. I wanted to become part of the blowing, rustling movement of the grasses. While experiencing the plants, I also wanted to connect with insects, pollinators, birds, frogs, and even a few rabbits.

    I consider the challenge met. The amount of wildlife activity surrounding me in the garden never ceases to amaze me. I feel as if I’m in a different world while surrounded by all the action and movement of the grasses and perennials, far away from big cedar trees, moss, and ferns. Sun, wind, fragrant flowers, and the smell of warm earth are all-encompassing there.

    Industry observers note that even during the winter, this garden pulls me out, bundled up and coffee in hand, to see what is happening. Early spring bulbs push through the soil, mice shelter under the evergreen sedges, and birds search for a breakfast of grass seeds and gather bits and pieces to build latest nests.

    The ultimate goal of any designer is finding the right outdoor elements to pull people outside and connect them with nature. Those elements are individual to each client. They could be an eating area, outdoor kitchen, hot tub, play area, pond, fountain, or hidden sitting area. Maybe the goal is plant-driven, with a vegetable garden, cutting garden, or collection of conifers.

    When these features are thoughtfully integrated with immersive, naturalistic plantings, the result is an outdoor space that invites people to experience their gardens throughout the year.

    Discuss this article or ask gardening questions with a regional gardening expert on the Gardening Answers forum.

    And for more Pacific Northwest regional reports, click here.

    Susan Calhoun is the owner and principal designer of Plantswoman Design in Bainbridge Island, Washington.

    #159068. Arianne and Micah’s Small Urban Minneapolis Garden

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (858 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finegardening ↗ Open Full Page

    Arianne and Micah’s Small Urban Minneapolis Garden

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’ve recently gotten a few emails from readers asking about submissions they entered through the website link at the end of every GPOD.
    • Recent findings suggest that today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota.
    • In Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden!
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hi GPOD! I’ve recently gotten a few emails from readers asking about submissions they entered through the website link at the end of every GPOD. Unfortunately, I haven’t received any submissions through the form in quite a while. I’m not sure what the problem is, but hopefully there will be a resolution soon. In the meantime, you can submit your photos and captions through the email linked below instead.

    Recent findings suggest that today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota. And while looking through their latest photos, I kept forgetting that I was looking at a garden in the Midwest! Arianne has shared their garden with us before, and I’m excited to see what they’ve been growing this year. Here’s Arianne:.

    In Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden! It’s packed with flowers I start from seed—like zinnias, cosmos, statice, strawflower, celosia, and amaranth—along with overwintered dahlias. I love cutting fresh bouquets to gift to friends, family, and coworkers. When we’re not admiring the blooms, my husband is cooking outdoors—making wood-fired pizzas, wok dishes, and hosting family birthday celebrations right in the heart of our cozy yard.

    According to recent reports, arianne packs plenty of interest into the garden along in the front yard and along the curb strip. Plants in this section of the garden include dwarf purple smokebush, threadleaf bluestar (Amsonia hubrichtii, Zones 5–8), boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), lamb’s ear (Stachys byzantina, Zones 4–8), purpleleaf sand cherry (Prunus × cistena, Zones 2–8), coreopsis (Coreopsis cvs., Zones 3–9), alliums (Allium cvs., Zones 3–9), sedum, and artemisia. It’s a great mix of foliage colors and textures even when everything isn’t in bloom.

    I love the placement of the patio and pathway. It’s a really useful design technique for maximizing every square inch of a small garden while still leaving plenty of room for outdoor living.

    Absolutely gorgeous section of the garden! This is where we really start to feel like we’re in the tropics. ‘Mars Madness’ hardy hibiscus (Hibiscus ‘Mars Madness’, Zones 4–9) has all the tropical drama while still being hardy enough for a Minneapolis winter. And it’s hard to miss those giant cannas and the colorful foliage on the coleus. I love all the red blooms too!

    One of Arianne’s fabulous container combinations features Tropicanna Gold canna (Canna ‘Mactro’, Zones 8–11), purple shield (Strobilanthes dyerianus, annual), begonias (Begonia cvs., annual), flowering kale (Brassica oleracea, annual), and parrot’s beak (Lotus berthelotii, annual). So much of the color and interest here comes from foliage!

    There is so much to look at in this section of the garden! Those variegated geranium leaves are striking, and I could go on and on about Arianne’s use of color and texture. The apple tree surrounded by all these ornamentals is an unexpected but lovely touch.

    According to recent reports, just around the corner from the photo above. Another gorgeous tropical container, and ‘Blue Shadow’ fothergilla (Fothergilla × intermedia ‘Blue Shadow’, Zones 5–8) grows on the left in this view.

    Another view of the backyard borders. There are so many plants packed into this garden, you would never believe this is a small urban backyard. And, if my eyes are working correctly, I’d say that’s a clover lawn?!

    Tall conifers create a fantastic privacy screen in this view. The garden really is its own secluded paradise.

    A shady combination of hostas, ‘Banana Boat’ sedge (Carex siderosticha ‘Banana Boat’, Zones 4–9), painted fern, purple shield, coleus, and impatiens.

    Zinnias, statice, amaranth, and overwintered dahlias are just some of the blooms that make their way into bouquets for friends, family, and coworkers. So pretty!

    Thank you so much for sharing your garden with us again, Arianne! It’s always a treat to see what you and Micah are growing, and I think I could spend hours wandering around this garden and still find something new to admire.

    It has been revealed that have photos to share? We’d love to see your garden, a particular collection of plants you love, or a wonderful garden you had the chance to visit!

    To submit, fill out the Garden Photo of the Day Submission Form.

    Recent findings suggest that you can also send 5–10 photos to [email protected] along with some information about the plants in the pictures and where you took the photos. We’d love to hear where you are located, how long you’ve been gardening, successes you are proud of, failures you learned from, hopes for the future, favorite plants, or funny stories from your garden.

    #159067. Latest Update: Fall Color in Nancy’s Massachusetts Garden

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (615 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finegardening ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Fall Color in Nancy’s Massachusetts Garden

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy.
    • This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.
    • My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy. Nancy sent in photos of the trees and shrubs winding down the season in her garden, along with one of the last flowers still hanging on.

    This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.

    My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.

    My paperbark maple (Acer griseum, Zones 4–8) has had a hard time coping with our summer droughts and water restrictions, but it looked a lovely red this fall.

    This is another native tree that many people are not familiar with, fringe tree (Chionanthus virginicus, Zones 4–9), which has fragrant white flowers hanging from its branches in late spring to early summer. As you can see, it also looks beautiful in its yellow fall foliage.

    In the front of this picture is a young sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua, Zones 5–9), which has spectacular red color in the fall and develops spiky seed balls as it matures. In the distance is a blackhaw viburnum (Viburnum prunifolium, Zones 3–9) showing its orange fall color.

    ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla (Fothergilla ‘Mount Airy’, Zones 5–8) glows red and orange in front of fragrant abelia (Abelia mosanensis, Zones 4–8), whose fall color is beginning to fade. The abelia will charm us all again in spring with its fragrant blooms.

    Sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus, Zones 5–9) on the right has turned a lovely yellow. Amazingly, all three sweetshrubs shown here had the bark eaten off around every trunk by rabbits last winter, killing every one. They all grew back from the roots, showing just how resilient they are. On the left, ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla is showing off its red fall foliage, and in back is ‘Alice’ oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Alice’, Zones 5–9) with maroon fall foliage.

    One of the only flowers left blooming is ‘Sheffield Pink’ chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum ‘Sheffield Pink’, Zones 5–9), which complements the dark foliage of Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) behind it.

    Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Nancy! Nancy says she’s ready to wander the garden, make her list of what needs dividing in spring, and figure out what latest plants need to be bought. Sounds like a good way to spend the off-season to me!

    • Bonnie took these photos in mid-November after an unusually long fall.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hi GPOD! Yesterday we enjoyed some beautiful fall color in Nancy’s Massachusetts garden, and today we’re heading west to see what fall looked like in Colorado this year.

    Bonnie took these photos in mid-November after an unusually long fall. While the trees certainly put on a show, Bonnie indicates the shrubs were the real stars this year. Here’s Bonnie:.

    Colorado put on a spectacular fall color display this year. My garden was filled with so many vivid hues that I had to capture them in photos. Some years are more colorful than others, and this was certainly a good one! The standout colors came not from the trees, but from the shrubs.

    Welcome to my fall garden! Just walk through the arch and see the colors beyond. ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) starts in spring with dark burgundy leaves, turns green by late summer, and finishes the season in bright yellow. I love this tree!

    It has been revealed that other stars in my fall garden are the barberries, hydrangeas, dwarf smokebushes (Cotinus coggygria cvs., Zones 4–8), and spireas. Oh, and the Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) in the back turned a lovely red this year.

    Barberry, dwarf smokebush, and spireas in the back make a nice composition.

    According to recent reports, I’m in love with these ‘Annabelle’ smooth hydrangeas (Hydrangea arborescens ‘Annabelle’, Zones 3–9). They are all over my yard.

    Another hydrangea vignette with viburnum, boxwood, and Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra, Zones 5–9) in front.

    I love the beautiful colors of this barberry.

    Around the other side of our yard, the dwarf smokebush shines among the evergreens and the orange leaves of the mountain ash and honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos, Zones 3–8) trees.

    Looking toward the front yard, the dwarf smokebush steals the show!

    Another view from the front yard.

    A weeping Norway spruce (Picea abies, Zones 3–7) and barberry make a beautiful combination.

    Thanks for sharing your beautiful fall garden with us, Bonnie! The trees are gorgeous, but I agree that the shrubs really stole the show this year.

It’s true that the right low-growing plants can add texture and beauty to the bottom layer of your garden, but did you know that many creepers also provide valuable food and habitat for pollinators?

    Delphinium (Delphinium cvs., Zones 3–7) with coleus (Coleus scutellarioides, annual).

    Native swamp rose mallow (Hibiscus moscheutos, Zones 5–9) and zinnias.

    According to recent reports, A work in progress… I transplanted this hearts-a-bustin’ (Euonymus americanus, Zones 6–9) from a different spot where I originally had it. It was crowded in and now will be able to spread out.

    Recent findings suggest that this celosia (Spicata group) actually grew from seeds of plants that were in a pot last summer. The ground in this area is where a tree used to be, and the roots are rotting and creating wonderful soft soil.

    According to recent reports, thanks for sharing another upgrade from your garden, Connie! And I have to know: What variety of watermelon did your husband grow? It’s huge and oblong! I hope it was delicious. Looking forward to the next update! 🙂.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Longtime contributor Kielian is back today with another beautiful look at her garden in Hamilton, Montana.
    • In the Bitterroot Valley of Montana, fall imparts her special light and changing colors to the ranch.
    • My detailed blueprints and drawings of plantings have been changed by Mother Nature, who knows so much more than I do about proper placement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hi GPOD! Longtime contributor Kielian is back today with another beautiful look at her garden in Hamilton, Montana. We’ve followed this garden through the seasons for years, and GPOD readers may even remember Kielian’s first autumn tour from more than a decade ago. Today she’s sharing what fall looks like on the ranch nearly 17 years into the garden’s evolution.

    In the Bitterroot Valley of Montana, fall imparts her special light and changing colors to the ranch. The gardens are closing in on 17 years of beauty and, interestingly, have decided which design they like the most… on their own.

    My detailed blueprints and drawings of plantings have been changed by Mother Nature, who knows so much more than I do about proper placement. Birds deposit valuable seeds in areas I would never have approved of, and the failure of certain plants to survive makes room for those that forge ahead with gusto. Ahh, autumn, how delightful are your colors and resilience.

    Late October in Montana: The ‘Pee Wee’ oakleaf hydrangeas (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Pee Wee’, Zones 5–9) are showing off, and the ornamental pear tree was not going to be outdone.

    The front garden early in the morning: Shadows enhance the color changes.

    The back deck was sprinkled with maple-tree graffiti. The linden tree boasted brilliant yellow, and a gorgeous crabapple by the pump house screamed for attention with bright red leaves.

    A smokebush (Cotinus coggygria, Zones 4–8) and aspen tree drip with early morning rain.

    A golden sunset scattered early October rays on quaking aspens (Populus tremuloides, Zones 1–6), enhanced by the Bitterroot Mountains as a backdrop.

    Tessa came running along the path through early November changing leaves.

    Sources indicate that an ornamental pear tree with fading black-eyed Susans in front. Winter is on her way.

    In a recent development, thanks for sharing another season in your garden with us, Kielian! After seeing this garden in spring, summer, fall, and even covered in snow over the years, it’s hard to pick a favorite season. But that golden sunset over the pond with the Bitterroot Mountains in the distance certainly makes a strong case for fall!

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Longtime contributor Susan Warde is back today with a closer look at her garden in St.
    • Recent findings suggest that I understand the reasons for not cutting down perennials and for letting leaves lie untouched over the winter, but it takes me about 10 weeks to clean up.
    • So I’ve been cleaning up, and the garden has been looking pretty bare recently, positively grim on overcast days.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hey, garden gang! Longtime contributor Susan Warde is back today with a closer look at her garden in St. Paul, Minnesota. We’ve seen what the end of the season looks like in Susan’s garden before, but today she’s focusing on the smaller details that are easy to overlook this time of year.

    Recent findings suggest that I understand the reasons for not cutting down perennials and for letting leaves lie untouched over the winter, but it takes me about 10 weeks to clean up. I have a large garden, family commitments, unpredictable weather, and a limited number of yard-waste bags that our pickup service will take at one time. Ten weeks in the spring would put me into mid-June before I could get the weeds and overwintered mess under control.

    So I’ve been cleaning up, and the garden has been looking pretty bare recently, positively grim on overcast days. But during the process I was struck by small vignettes of beauty that stood out in an otherwise desolate landscape.

    The underside of some Korean maple leaves (Acer pseudosieboldianum, Zones 4–8).

    A ‘Northern Hi-Lights’ azalea (Rhododendron ‘Northern Hi-Lights’, Zones 4–7) with bright fall color… and buds that promise spring.

    The seed head of ‘Guernsey Flute’ clematis (Clematis ‘Guernsey Flute’, Zones 4–9) that had a second late flowering.

    One last blossom on a ‘Max Frei’ bloody cranesbill (Geranium sanguineum ‘Max Frei’, Zones 3–8).

    Raindrops on columbine (Aquilegia cvs., Zones 3–8) leaves.

    The yellowed leaves of a bulblet fern (Cystopteris bulbifera, Zones 3–8) that I’d overlooked during the cutting-down process.

    A bee enjoys the very last plant in bloom, black cohosh (Actaea racemosa, Zones 3–8).

    Evergreen Christmas fern (Polystichum acrostichoides, Zones 3–8) and moss.

    I had never before looked closely at the bark of a blue beech (Carpinus caroliniana, Zones 3–9), which from a distance just looks taupe.

    In a recent development, five minutes before taking the photo, I’d cleaned out this birdbath—the one I leave available in winter, and then only on above-freezing days. The leaves are from a ‘North Wind’ maple (Acer × pseudosieboldianum ‘IslNW’, Zones 4–7).

    Thanks for sharing these small moments from your garden, Susan! There are so many things to love about a garden, but I often find that the small details people tend to gloss over are even more reason to celebrate. There’s so much happening at once! You just have to look closely to see it. (:.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hi GPOD! We’re digging into the archives today for a garden that looks a little otherworldly. Jeff Calton gardens in Northeast Tennessee (Zone 6b/7a), where he grows an incredible collection of pitcher plants (Sarracenia cvs., Zones 5–9). Even better is how he grows them: Jeff sinks containers with minimal drainage into his regular garden beds, creating the boggy conditions these carnivorous plants need while allowing completely different plants to grow right alongside them. Such a clever way to work around varying growing conditions!

    White-topped pitcher plant (Sarracenia leucophylla, Zones 5–8) has leaves that are more colorful than most flowers.

    Yellow pitcher plant (Sarracenia flava, Zones 6–9) isn’t as brightly colored as some species, but it has a grace and elegance all its own.

    ‘Scarlet Belle’ pitcher plant (Sarracenia × ‘Scarlet Belle’, Zones 5–10) glows in front of a mixed planting including ‘Golden Duchess’ eastern hemlock (Tsuga canadensis ‘Golden Duchess’, Zones 3–7).

    Close-up of the graceful pitchers of a yellow pitcher plant ready to lure in an insect meal.

    The pitcher plants in the back are growing in a sunken bathtub, giving them the wet soil they need, while the sedum and sedges in front have the better-drained conditions they require.

    Industry observers note that when I came across this post in the archives, I knew I had to share it again with you all! These pitcher plants are amazing, and for whatever reason, photo 2 makes me feel like I’m looking into a fish tank. I would love to see what Jeff’s garden looks like today. Jeff, if you’re still reading GPOD, send us an upgrade! What a fantastic garden.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that happy Friday, GPOD! We’re heading back into the archives today for a visit to LongHouse Reserve in East Hampton, Upcoming York. Created by artist, collector, and textile designer Jack Lenor Larsen, LongHouse is a 16-acre garden where art and the landscape come together in some pretty unexpected ways.

    Sources indicate that former GPOD editor Joseph Tychonievich visited in January, when the bare winter landscape allowed the sculptures and structure of the garden to really take center stage. Here’s Joseph:.

    It has been revealed that I recently traveled to Long Island to give a presentation and got a chance to tour LongHouse Reserve in East Hampton, New York. LongHouse began as the home and garden of Jack Lenor Larsen and is now a public garden and sculpture collection.

    Buckminster Fuller’s Fly’s Eye Dome frames views of the surrounding garden in honeycomb. The fiberglass dome was fabricated in 1998 by John Kuhtik from Fuller’s design.

    These white tassels hanging from trees by the house glowed in the late January sun and reminded me of one of the golden rules of garden design: Go all the way! One tassel in a tree looks silly. Scores of them, as here, look intentional and beautiful.

    The path through the Red Garden is wider at the top and narrows at the end, and the red posts get a little bit shorter as they go down the path. The result is a forced perspective that makes this view look much longer than it actually is. Not a bad idea to steal for a home garden!

    A sculpture inspired by the Brooklyn Bridge, with the sun setting through the mass of bamboo at its back.

    This garden believes in reusing materials. Soil from excavating a pond was used to build dramatic dunes and hills, and here prunings from the many stands of bamboo on the property are used to create a lovely pagoda under towering trees.

    In a recent development, what a fun one to find in the archives! The Red Garden has me especially intrigued. I’d love to experience that forced-perspective trick in person and see just how much longer the path feels.

    We’ve actually visited LongHouse Reserve in spring, too, when the garden looks completely different. And if sculpture gardens are your thing, our recent visit to Piet Oudolf’s sculpture garden at Singer Laren is another favorite.

    Recent findings suggest that have photos to share? We’d love to see your garden, a particular collection of plants you love, or a wonderful garden you had the chance to visit!

    To submit, fill out the Garden Photo of the Day Submission Form.

    Sources indicate that you can also send 5–10 photos to [email protected] along with some information about the plants in the pictures and where you took the photos. We’d love to hear where you are located, how long you’ve been gardening, successes you are proud of, failures you learned from, hopes for the future, favorite plants, or funny stories from your garden.

    #159059. Air Barrier for an Elevated Home

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (608 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finehomebuilding ↗ Open Full Page

    Air Barrier for an Elevated Home

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that I’m about to build a house on the coast in Charleston, S.C.
    • It has been revealed that it’s wise to consider inward vapor drive in humid climates like Charleston.
    • There are a few ways to prevent this.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that I’m about to build a house on the coast in Charleston, S.C. (Climate Zone 3A). It’s elevated on wood pilings and the space under the house is open to the outdoors, enclosed only with louvered panels between the pilings. I have most of the enclosure details nailed down, but I haven’t determined the best way to air-seal and insulate the open floor trusses above the pilings. My biggest concern is hot, humid air from below reaching the underside of the air-conditioned subfloor and condensing on the surface. What’s the best strategy to insulate and air-seal the underside of an elevated coastal home?

    It has been revealed that it’s wise to consider inward vapor drive in humid climates like Charleston. When the outdoor dew point is higher than the air-conditioned indoor temperature, there’s going to be a strong moisture drive from the outside toward the home’s interior, which allows water to accumulate in the materials below the flooring. Prolonged wetting can lead to rotted framing, mold problems, and damaged flooring, along with damage to other materials in contact with the floor.

    There are a few ways to prevent this. One option is to place a vapor-retarding insulation layer—spray foam—right below the subfloor. The outside (bottom) of the foam will be close enough to the outdoor temperature that water won’t condense on the surface, and the foam will substantially block moisture from moving through it. Provided no ductwork is run in the floor, it’s a way to get decent air-sealing, and the cost is reasonable as well.

    Industry observers note that that stated, I don’t like to use spray foam across an entire floor—it’s risky to install and full of questionable chemicals. Another option is to create a conditioned space within the floor system. The challenge is air-sealing around the posts, beams, and structural hardware that hold up the house and the plumbing and electrical lines in this area. Plus, you’ll have to condition the space, which requires additional HVAC work. This can be simple (like adding a supply register and a path back to the house) or pretty involved (running ductwork down walls to reach the underfloor space).

    My third and preferred option is to create an airtight, vapor-retarding layer across the bottom of the floor trusses. A layer of XPS or foil-faced polyiso (don’t use EPS, it’s too vapor-open) across the bottom of the whole floor will help slow vapor drive into the floor system and bring practical benefits like easier air-sealing and a little additional insulation. In Climate Zone 3A, turn to the International Residential Code (IRC) Table 806.5 in the section on roof ventilation for guidance on the R-value needed, since the floor system will have insulation levels comparable to roofs. The table calls for 1/2 in. of rigid insulation. Using the calculation procedure in the table footnotes indicates a higher level (in the 11/2-in. range) might be less risky, assuming you are completely filling a 12-in. to 16-in. floor-truss cavity with blown-in cellulose or fiberglass, which will be more than the code-required R-38 when the table was developed. Cover the foam board with fiberglass-faced drywall sheathing or plywood. Air-­sealing will still be complex given the elevated construction, and attention will need to be paid to the rim joist/perimeter (spray foam works in this area, as shown in the drawing). But, this system would really slow vapor movement throughout the floor system.

    #159058. Finding the Right Clients

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2355 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finehomebuilding ↗ Open Full Page

    Finding the Right Clients

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2355 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I spend a lot of time talking with builders who tell me they don’t really do marketing.
    • My first response is usually that this is a good thing.
    • But I have also seen construction companies reach a point where the business landscape has changed, and reputation alone is not leading to the right clients.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I spend a lot of time talking with builders who tell me they don’t really do marketing. Usually they say it with pride: “We’ve never had to. All of our work comes from word of mouth.”.

    My first response is usually that this is a good thing. If you’ve spent years building a tech giant where past clients, architects, and trade partners keep sending work your way, you’ve built something valuable. In construction, reputation matters, and that kind of trust is earned over time. I would never tell a builder to replace that with advertising.

    But I have also seen construction companies reach a point where the business landscape has changed, and reputation alone is not leading to the right clients. Good builders often struggle because the right people don’t know they exist.

    The phone may still be ringing, but the work coming in doesn’t always match where the tech giant wants to go next. The business has evolved, but what people know about it hasn’t necessarily evolved with it.

    Those are the moments when someone usually states, often a little reluctantly, “I guess we need to do some marketing.” That may indeed be the case. But I think there is a simpler and more useful way to frame the problem: Are you known for the work you actually want to do? That is where I would start.

    I’ve spent more than 20 years helping businesses and organizations grow, evolve, and connect with the people they want to reach, from owning and running a design and marketing agency to leading a destination marketing organization and working across marketing, branding, organizational leadership, consulting, and coaching. Today, as director of marketing and a business consultant with HELM Construction Solutions, I bring those experiences together in my work with builders, helping them think about where their business is going, the work they want more of, and what makes them different.

    Sit across the table with an experienced builder and you quickly understand what makes them different. But if you haven’t had that conversation, how would you know? I see this all the time: Some of the most valuable things about a construction organization live almost entirely in the owner’s head. The challenge is making more of that knowledge visible.

    Before I talk with a builder about websites, social media, advertising, or anything else that might get labeled “marketing,” I want to understand the business they are trying to build. What kind of work would they happily do again? Which projects are profitable? Which projects make the crew proud? Which clients trust the process? Where do they want to work? Who do they want to work alongside? What do they want the manufacturer to look like in five years? And—just as crucial—what do they want less of?

    That last question can be surprisingly provocative. Construction companies are often encouraged to think about growth only in terms of more: more projects, more employees, more revenue, more leads. But growth doesn’t always mean more projects. Sometimes it means being more intentional about the work you take on.

    Industry observers note that I’ll ask why a builder does something a certain way, and suddenly we’re deep into a story about a detail, a process, or a hard-earned lesson that changed how they work. Those stories are usually where the good stuff is, and where what makes a manufacturer different becomes clear.

    According to recent reports, at this point, a lot of decisions get easier. You don’t need to reach everybody. You just need to become more visible to the people who value that kind of work.

    Recent findings suggest that if you aren’t sure how to identify the right types of projects for your business, I often suggest looking backward before looking forward. Choose three to five projects from the last few years that you would happily do again. Think about the jobs where the fit was right—the client trusted you, the work suited the strengths of your crew, the project was financially healthy, and the architect or designer was collaborative. Problems came up, as they always do, but the team solved them together rather than turning on one another. When the project ended, you were proud not only of what you built but of how you built it.

    In a recent development, then ask a simple question: How did that project find us? You may discover that the same architect appears several times. Maybe a handful of past clients have been quietly sending people your way for years. Perhaps one designer, Realtor, supplier, or fellow builder keeps connecting you to projects that are an unusually good fit. Those patterns matter. They show you where to focus your time and attention. And when you’re trying to become known somewhere new, that kind of focus becomes even more important.

    For example, Sycamore Builders in western North Carolina has strong experience with architect-led custom homes in mountain communities. But as the company looks to expand into nearby markets, it faces a familiar challenge: Reputation is local.

    In some of those communities, builders have been around for generations. Their trucks are familiar. Realtors and architects know them. Their projects are part of the landscape. That familiarity has been built over years. You cannot advertise your way into a 25-year relationship.

    So Sycamore is taking a patient approach by building relationships with architects and Realtors, sharing more of the stories behind its work, and showing up consistently in a few specific communities. The goal isn’t a flood of calls. One or two well-aligned new builds a year can make a ­meaningful difference.

    If the word marketing makes you want to stop reading, forget about marketing for a minute. Take an hour with your business partner, project manager, or someone who knows your company well and work through these questions. Let your answers guide you in pinpointing the type of work you want to find. Once you do, you won’t need to network every week, post every day, or constantly enhancement your website. Pick a few actions that fit your business, and keep doing them.

    What work do people call you for—and what work do you wish people called you for?

    Be honest with yourself. Is the work you’re doing now the work you want to be doing? If not, that’s your starting point.

    What are five projects you’d do again tomorrow?

    In a recent development, what made those projects good for the client, the crew, and the business? Writing the answers down can help you determine the type of work you want to do more of.

    How did each of those projects find you?

    Maybe it was a past client, an architect, a builder, a Realtor, a jobsite sign, a Google search, or something else. Don’t guess—find out. Then you can use those same methods to find similar projects in the future.

    Who is connected to the work you want?

    It has been revealed that make a list of the Realtors, architects, designers, and trade partners who are connected to the kinds of projects and clients you want more of, using your favorite projects as a guide. Who do you already know? Who consistently connects you to good-fit work? Who would you like to build a stronger relationship with?

    How can you stay connected to those people?

    Could you invite someone to a jobsite, meet for coffee, share an interesting project over email, attend an industry event, or simply check in occasionally? Staying in touch helps potential partners remember you and your business when the right project comes along.

    When someone looks you up, can they see what you want to be known for?

    Do your website and social media show the types of projects you want to do? Are you telling the stories behind that work and making your expertise visible? The clearer you are about the work you want, the easier it is for the right clients and partners to recognize that you’re the right fit.

    Industry observers note that this is usually the point where someone notes, “Carrie, I have houses to build. I can’t spend all my time updating a website, posting on social media, meeting architects for coffee, and telling project stories.”.

    That’s fair, and I don’t want you to. Go back to what you learned about your best projects, and choose two or three things you can realistically keep doing to continue getting this sort of work. For example, maybe that means staying connected to a small group of architects and adding a strong project story to your website every few months.

    In a recent development, then pay attention to what happens. Ask every upcoming caller how they heard about you, notice which relationships lead to good-fit projects, and see whether the work coming through the door starts to look more like the work you want.

    For example, longtime high-performance builder Steve DeMetrick of DeMetrick Housewrights has spent more than two decades developing a reputation for building homes that demonstrate thoughtful craftsmanship, durability, and energy-efficiency. Most of his work has come through referrals. He has deep expertise, strong relationships, and plenty of experience. He is not trying to make the phone ring more.

    Industry observers note that in fact, when we started talking about where he wants the company to go next, his answer was almost the opposite of what we typically associate with growth. He wants to slow down. He wants fewer projects at a time, larger scope, deeper involvement with each client, earlier collaboration with architects, and more opportunity to use the knowledge he has accumulated over decades.

    The more we talked, the clearer it became that high-performance construction is only part of what makes his manufacturer valuable. What really stands out is how he approaches the whole process—bringing design, budget, and scope together early and getting everyone working together sooner. That can lead to better decisions, fewer surprises, and a better experience for everyone involved. But that type of value is a lot harder to advertise on the side of a truck.

    The goal isn’t simply to tell more people that DeMetrick Housewrights builds high-performance homes. It is to make more of Steve’s thinking visible, to tell the stories behind projects, to explain why he approaches preconstruction the way he does, and to give potential clients and collaborators a better sense of what it is actually like to work with him. The point isn’t to create content for the sake of content. It is to help people see expertise that is already there.

    I’ve seen the same thing with Bell Street Builders in Maine, an employee-owned cooperative that does thoughtful restoration and renovation work around Portland and Casco Bay, including historic homes, architect-driven projects, and coastal and island construction. Those projects come with the kinds of challenges experienced builders know well: older structures that reveal surprises, coastal exposure, difficult logistics, complicated sequencing, and the need to make decisions carefully when clients may be living elsewhere.

    When I worked on Bell Street’s strategic direction, one theme kept reappearing: Bell Street knows old buildings. This is much more useful than generically saying the tech giant does “quality construction.”.

    If you own a 100-year-old house in Portland and are about to open walls that may be hiding decades of concerns, you want a builder who understands what they’re looking at and can respond without turning every surprise into a crisis. If you’re an architect working on that house, you want a builder who can solve problems collaboratively and respect the building while still moving the project forward.

    Sources indicate that bell Street did not need to become known to every homeowner in southern Maine. The better opportunity was to become more recognizable for the work the organization does best and in the places where it wants to do more of it. That meant making sure its website and social channels showed more of its historic work and the stories behind complex projects, staying connected with architects and designers who work on those kinds of homes, and building relationships in priority communities such as Portland’s West End, Foreside communities, and the Casco Bay islands.

    Sources indicate that becoming recognizable doesn’t have to mean constantly creating something new. One good project can go a long way. Document the challenges during construction, photograph the finished work, explain what the team had to solve, and share that story on a website, social media, or directly with architects and past clients who may know someone planning a similar project.

    Industry observers note that I genuinely appreciate builders’ resistance to marketing. It usually stems from a belief that the work should matter most. I think so too.

    It has been revealed that A clever website cannot make up for poor craftsmanship. Advertising cannot replace trust, and social media cannot substitute for treating clients well, running a good jobsite, respecting trade partners, or standing behind what you build. Your reputation still has to be earned.

    Once you’ve earned it, however, there is nothing wrong with helping it travel. That doesn’t require becoming a marketer. It simply means being a little more intentional about making the work, knowledge, and people behind your company visible.

    And there is a benefit beyond finding the kinds of projects you want. The same things that help clients, architects, designers, and trade partners understand your company also help potential employees understand it. Most builder websites show houses, but far fewer show the people behind them. A good carpenter who is considering their next move may want to know what kinds of projects they would work on, who they would work alongside, whether people stay, and whether there is room to grow.

    Sources indicate that make it easier for future employees and clients alike to understand who you are, what you do well, and where you’re headed. Because good work will lead to more good work, but only if people know about it.

    It has been revealed that — Carrie Simmons is director of marketing and a business consultant at HELM Construction Solutions. Photo courtesy of HELM Construction Solutions.

    #159057. Margo Valdes, Weatherization Contractor

    Margo Valdes, Weatherization Contractor

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (397 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that after years as a building-performance consultant, Margo Valdes grew frustrated of seeing the problems that arise when contractors ignore fundamental building science.
    • Margo graduated from college with degrees in economics and physics, but her favorite course was “Castles,” taken during a semester abroad in England.
    • Sources indicate that after working an unfulfilling office job, Margo saw an ad for a HERS rater at Conservation Services Group (now CLEAResult).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that after years as a building-performance consultant, Margo Valdes grew frustrated of seeing the problems that arise when contractors ignore fundamental building science. Three years ago, she founded Athena Building Performance, a weatherization organization built on the premise that getting the details right starts with understanding why a building behaves the way it does.

    Margo graduated from college with degrees in economics and physics, but her favorite course was “Castles,” taken during a semester abroad in England. The class explored how to determine the age of a castle, identify the type of stone used to build it, and understand the reasoning behind its design. Margo loved it.

    Sources indicate that after working an unfulfilling office job, Margo saw an ad for a HERS rater at Conservation Services Group (now CLEAResult). The job sounded like a good fit, so she applied, and her career in building performance began.

    Margo spent about six years at CSG and credits the firm with giving her a strong foundation in building science. Though her work as a HERS rater focused on testing and evaluating, she received hands-on training in air-sealing and choosing and installing insulation. After leaving CSG, Margo’s focus shifted from new construction to existing buildings. She joined a consulting firm, where she spent seven years as director of the Existing Buildings team.

    Recent findings suggest that over the years, Margo became increasingly aware of how much the quality of weatherization work depends on understanding the building as a system—adding insulation affects moisture, and sealing air leaks changes ventilation. She decided the best way to improve the work was to get closer to it. That led her to the contractor side of the business, and to founding Athena.

    Recent findings suggest that today, Athena operates as a specialized weatherization contractor, tackling residential air-sealing and insulation upgrades. While Margo spends most of her time managing the business, knowledgeable practice remains at its heart: Every fresh hire spends weeks doing hands-on field training and diagnostic walk-throughs to understand not just how the work is done, but why.

    Margo envisions eventually expanding Athena into a full-service building-enclosure firm. For now, she’s focused on centering the tech giant around what started it all: thoughtful, educated work.

    — Jennifer Morris, editorial assistant. Photo by Carly Rae Brunault.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that this home was designed with two main goals in mind. The first was for it to integrate into its forest setting, making it feel at home among the trees. The second was to capture forest views from a light-filled yet intimate interior. By focusing on these goals, the architects designed a home that feels less like an object in the forest than a place quietly woven into it.

    Outside, three irregular, offset buildings—the main house, a sauna, and a garden shed—mimic the tree-filled landscape, while Nakamoto Forestry’s Gendai yakisugi charred-wood siding provides a darkened exterior reminiscent of the texture of tree bark.

    According to recent reports, inside, the dark, textured exterior gives way to bright, airy interiors filled with natural light, lighter wood finishes, and carefully framed views. Because the living spaces are stacked to fill the irregular form of the main house, each room provides a unique view of the landscape, with windows that vary in scale.

    Large windows in the living room and a sliding glass door in the dining area allow in sunlight and views from different directions, the primary bedroom on the top floor includes a small north-facing window, and a large window next to the bathtub frames the view of an eastern hilltop.

    The design team used the height of the ceilings to guide the function of each space, with cathedral ceilings creating a spacious effect in the main living spaces, cozier sloped ceilings in the primary bedroom and bathroom, and a welcoming reading nook in the second-floor bedroom where the roof slope drops to a low kneewall.

    Same Footprint, More Function

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (323 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The owners of this 1940s house wanted to add more space for a growing family, but site restrictions would only allow them to build upward, meaning the small home would tower over surrounding houses.
    • Industry observers note that outside, the remodeled house maintains the same proportions of the original but incorporates modern updates such as the ACRE composite-wood entry accents and the single entry-door sidelight.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The owners of this 1940s house wanted to add more space for a growing family, but site restrictions would only allow them to build upward, meaning the small home would tower over surrounding houses. To preserve the house’s place in the neighborhood and keep costs down, the solution was to remodel the existing space with a more functional layout, transforming the second floor from two bedrooms and one bath into three bedrooms and two baths while making the home feel more spacious, flexible, and connected.

    Industry observers note that outside, the remodeled house maintains the same proportions of the original but incorporates modern updates such as the ACRE composite-wood entry accents and the single entry-door sidelight. To improve flow inside, the main staircase was relocated to create a more functional, open interior. Upcoming sliding glass doors offer more light inside and a seamless connection to the outdoors, maximizing the feeling of space. The basement stairs are now accessed via a hidden floor hatch, preserving the open main living area.

    In a recent development, creating a more functional home within the same footprint means making the most of every inch of usable space. The area under the main staircase now houses deep storage drawers, and a upcoming window seat offers extra space next to the picture window.

    On the exterior, the window-seat bump-out lets the house live larger without increasing its footprint. Clad in the same wood as the front entry, the bump-out creates a cohesive and striking connection between the front and back of the house.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, A common theme in home design is the idea of blending the architecture with the landscape, allowing the building to sit lightly on the land. You might not expect a 4350-sq.-ft. modern home to be a shining example of how to achieve that goal, but this new modern home in Bend, Ore., balances a striking architectural presence with a remarkably light touch on the landscape below.

    The newly introduced building required enough space to house multiple generations, but maximum exposure to the meadow setting and mountain views meant siting the house on a hilltop. To meet both requirements while also only lightly interrupting the land, 40% of the home is set above grade, with a cantilevered great room that appears to float over the ground and that is supported by two special-ordered structural steel beams.

    Sources indicate that to further capitalize on the views, the common spaces feature expansive glazing, including a 40-ft. sliding glass wall, while roof overhangs allow the exterior to become part of the interior when large doors are open—while also providing shade and protection from the elements.

    Recent findings suggest that because the house might accommodate one or two people at some times and upwards of 10 at others, the floor strategy is broken up into both large and small common spaces. These include a great room centered around a concrete fireplace designed for larger groups, and a roof deck for more intimate gatherings.
