    "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press": "Ambiguous Evidence: Enjoining Repetition of Libels"

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1272 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I'm serializing my upcoming Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the third and last Part:.
    • Throughout much of American history, the dominant view has been that courts can't enjoin libels.
    • Industry observers note that yet since then, many state courts have allowed permanent injunctions against libels.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I'm serializing my upcoming Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the third and last Part:.

    Throughout much of American history, the dominant view has been that courts can't enjoin libels. The first precedent on this was Brandreth v. Lance (1839), an 1839 New York trial court decision. This was followed by State ex rel. Liversey v. Judge (1882), an 1882 Louisiana Supreme Court decision. Subsequent decisions helped establish this as a firm rule, seemingly culminating in Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson.

    Industry observers note that yet since then, many state courts have allowed permanent injunctions against libels. By my count the court systems of thirty-four states have either so held or have in practice been so acting, with only six states plus D.C. continuing to categorically bar such injunctions. {See Eugene Volokh, Anti-Libel Injunctions, 168 U. Pa. L. Rev. 73 (2019).}.

    This trend seems to have accelerated with the rise of the internet. Historically, a libel has been a short, sharp shock—typically, a one-time article in a newspaper that is printed and can't be removed—with the only possible remedy being damages or criminal prosecution. But the internet can turn libel into a steady drip, drip, drip of damage, with more readers seeing a libelous web page every day. Injunctions thus seem a more useful remedy.

    The internet also makes it easier for judgment-proof defendants to cause real damage; an injunction can thus be useful in a way that a damages remedy might not be. Criminal libel is theoretically available in about ten states, and there are indeed likely a couple of dozen criminal libel prosecutions in the United States each year. But in most states the only way to deploy criminal remedies in service of protecting reputation is through getting an injunction that can be enforced through the threat of criminal contempt.

    Are these injunctions contrary to the original meaning of the First Amendment? The answer turns out to be complicated, especially if we focus on permanent injunctions, entered to forbid the repetition of material found to be libelous in a final judgment (with the defendant having had an opportunity to call for a jury trial).

    It's true that early sources often view the freedom of the press as precluding prior restraints: To quote William Blackstone, "The liberty of the press is indeed essential to the nature of a free state: but this consists in laying no previous restraints upon publications, and not in freedom from censure for criminal matter when published." Yet this doesn't quite speak to the modern question whether the law may restrain repetition of material for matter found to be criminal (or tortious).

    Industry observers note that nor does it speak to whether the law may require removal of such matter after a trial: Removal just wasn't practically an option in the print era. In such situations of injunctions against repetition of an already published libel or ordering its removal, "[e]very freeman" would retain the "undoubted right to lay what sentiments he pleases before the public" (again quoting Blackstone) at least in the first instance.

    Nor is there a "restrictive power of a licenser" or "control of an inspector" in the sense that the Framers likely understood licensers, which is to say officials administering a licensing system. (To quote St. George Tucker, under that system "all books printed were previously licensed by some of the great offices of state, or the two universities, and all foreign books were exposed to a similar scrutiny before they were vended.") The injunction is imposed by a judge, often following a jury verdict, administering justice between two parties, not running a traditional licensing system that "subject[s] all freedom of sentiment to the prejudices of one man, and make[s] him the arbitrary and infallible judge of all controverted points in learning, religion, and government.".

    According to recent reports, likewise, early sources stressed the importance of allowing a jury to resolve what is true and false in libel cases. But, as I noted, the modern permanent injunction in libel cases is entered after a final judgment on the merits, which at least in principle allows a defendant to demand a jury trial. If the defendant has so demanded, then any injunction would be based on the jury verdict.

    According to recent reports, this stems in part from the twentieth-century merger of law and equity, since equitable remedies, such as injunctions, can now be issued following the use of the legal procedure of a jury trial. (Historically, one argument against injunctions in libel cases has been that "equity will not enjoin a libel," a statement about the limits of the equity courts more than about constitutional protections for free expression.) Indeed, the Delaware Court of Chancery, which operates in a state system where law and equity remain largely separate, has continued to hold that it generally can't enjoin libel. But it expressly left open the possibility that, once the Delaware Superior Court (the law court) concludes—after a jury trial, if the parties don't choose a bench trial—that a statement is libelous, an injunction can then be issued.

    In a recent development, in practice, anti-libel injunctions are often parts of default judgments, or follow bench trials, and thus don't involve factual findings by juries. In both those situations, though, the defendant can be said to have waived his right to a jury trial. To be sure, temporary restraining orders and preliminary injunctions are entered before any opportunity for a jury trial—but for that reason many courts continue to reject them on First Amendment grounds.

    And, as the California Supreme Court held in allowing such post-final-judgment permanent injunctions, the reasoning of Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson expressly sets aside injunctions in traditional civil libel disputes:.

    The high court was careful to point out … that the statute being considered was "not aimed at the redress of individual or private wrongs. Remedies for libel remain available and unaffected." … But most significant is that the court … clarified that it was not addressing "questions as to the extent of authority to prevent publications in order to protect private rights according to the principles governing the exercise of the jurisdiction of courts of equity." In a footnote, the court cited [an] … article by Roscoe Pound that observed that English courts permit "an injunction in case the libel was repeated or publication was continued after a jury had found the matter libelous." Therefore, Near expressly did not address the issue posed in the present case.

    The Supreme Court hasn't confronted such permanent injunctions against repetition of proven libel since Near, but it has authorized injunctions against obscenity (which Near had anticipated) and against commercial speech that proposes illegal transactions. The one case in which it granted certiorari as to anti-libel injunctions, Tory v. Cochran (2005), largely disappeared when the plaintiff, famed lawyer Johnnie Cochran, died while the case was pending. None of these cases discussed the original meaning of the First Amendment, and the lower court cases dealing with the matter have largely not discussed it, either.

    So here we have a fairly rich body of originalist evidence related to libel law generally. We have a considerable body of evidence from before and shortly after the Framing that talks about "previous restraints." And we have some nineteenth-century sources that seem to take the view that all injunctions in libel cases are unconstitutional. But how exactly do the Framing-era sources apply to a permanent anti-libel injunction issued by a court following the resolution of a libel case? Hard to know for sure.

    Aiper Scuba V3 Ultra Review: Nearly Perfect Pool Cleaning

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (491 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Bobvila

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Sources indicate that I’ve tested several Aiper cleaners over the years, and the Aiper Scuba V3 Ultra feels like a natural evolution of the brand’s previous models.
    • It has been revealed that what impressed me right away was just how much the Scuba V3 Ultra can do in one cleaning cycle.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    Sources indicate that I’ve tested several Aiper cleaners over the years, and the Aiper Scuba V3 Ultra feels like a natural evolution of the brand’s previous models. I ran it through repeated cleaning cycles in my 8,500-gallon saltwater pool in Florida, where leaves, bugs, fine debris, and the occasional patch of algae give pool robots plenty to deal with. Setup was super simple: The Aiper app connected quickly, the robot updated without any fuss, and I had it in the water about 15 minutes after opening the box.

    It has been revealed that what impressed me right away was just how much the Scuba V3 Ultra can do in one cleaning cycle. Plenty of the robotic pool cleaners we’ve tested at Bob Vila handle floors, walls, and the waterline, but only a select few can also skim floating debris from the surface. That matters in my open-air pool, which regularly collects bugs and leaves. Anything the Aiper actually reaches gets cleaned extremely well.

    The MicroMesh filter is another highlight. It traps extremely fine material, including algae and sediment that can slip through coarser filter baskets. Cleaning that ultra-fine layer takes a little more effort—I usually spend a few minutes thoroughly rinsing it with a hose and then leave it out to dry—but that’s a fair trade-off for how much fine material it captures. The app is also among the better pool-cleaner apps I’ve used, and I like getting a notification when the cleaning cycle is finished. The robot then floats neatly near the pool edge for retrieval.

    Where the V3 Ultra disappointed me was its claim of shallow-area cleaning. Aiper notes it can work in water down to about 7.9 inches deep, but my sun shelf is apparently too shallow for it to clean reliably. I still have to brush debris from the shelf into the main pool and let the robot collect it there. It also won’t clean my pool steps. For a $2,300 machine marketed around near-total pool coverage, those are significant omissions—especially since sun shelves have become so common in newer pools.

    It has been revealed that still, I’m a fan of the Scuba V3 Ultra overall. My older Aiper cleaner has been running reliably for close to two years, which gives me more confidence in the brand than I’d have from a short-term test alone. The voice assistant is useful without being obnoxious, retrieval is simple, filtration is excellent, and cleaning performance everywhere the robot can reach is phenomenal. I’m still waiting for the robot that will truly clean every inch of my pool, but the Scuba V3 Ultra gets closer than most.

    The Best Mops for Wood Floors, Tested and Reviewed

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
    • According to recent reports, hardwood floors are a coveted classic for their diverse graining and beautiful colors that add richness and dimension to so many decor schemes.
    • If maintained properly—and that means having the right tool—wood flooring can hold its finish for years without damage or cracking.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    According to recent reports, hardwood floors are a coveted classic for their diverse graining and beautiful colors that add richness and dimension to so many decor schemes. But in homes with children, pets, and/or heavy traffic, hardwood floors are prone to showing dirt and dust quickly.

    If maintained properly—and that means having the right tool—wood flooring can hold its finish for years without damage or cracking. Some brooms, for instance, can be too abrasive, whereas mops designed to clean hardwood floors are ideal for these surfaces.

    It can be tricky to pick a floor mop that suits your cleaning style and budget, as well as the degree of dirt and stains on your flooring. Our top pick, Mr. Siga Professional Microfiber Mop for Wood Floors, was easy to use and cleaned our floors quickly and thoroughly. To help you find the best mop for your situation, we put a host of different products through their paces in a home with plenty of dust, dirt, and pet hair. We also spoke to professionals like Ryan Knoll, owner of Tidy Casa in Scottsdale, Arizona, to get a bit of expert knowledge on what shoppers will want to look for in a mop. Read on to see what to look for in the best mops for wood floors, as well as our reviews of products we deem superior in today’s crowded market.

    Bottom line: Discover the best mops for wood floors, tested for performance and ease of use, to keep your hardwood looking pristine.

    Many do not know what to look for in the best mops for hardwood floors, but here are some real-life reviews to get you started. Check out the following models, all of which met our criteria for quality, ease of use, and overall performance, to find the best mops for wood flooring for your particular needs.

    Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5;Effectiveness 4/5; Maneuverability 5/5; Value 5/5.

    Though Mr.Siga wasn’t an immediately recognizable brand, we were delightfully surprised by the excellent job its Professional Microfiber Mop did in testing. We found that this tall floor mop with an adjustable stainless steel telescoping handle had great reach under dusty couches and around table legs. The very wide rectangular mophead with a 360-degree swivel action meant less work on large hardwood floors, since with fewer swipes and greater maneuverability, we got our dusting and wet-mopping jobs done quickly.

    Industry observers note that at first, we were stumped on how to moisten the cleaning cloth, but a bit of online research taught us a few tricks for microfiber mops. Simply wet the cloth, roll it up to wring it out, then attach it to the mophead base. The microfiber mop cloths are reusable—just toss in the washing machine to launder. A handy dirt scrubber attachment is included for tight corners and tough grime, and the mop can be used on a variety of surfaces, including marble, tile, and laminate, as well as hardwood.

    What our tester indicates: “This pick’s wide, swiveling mophead helped us clean large floors with fewer passes, and the adjustable handle made it easy to reach under furniture.”—Stephanie Cronk, Product Reviews tester and writer.

    Get the Mr.Siga microfiber mop for wood floors at Amazon.

    Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5;Effectiveness 4/5; Maneuverability 4/5; Value 5/5.

    According to recent reports, when quick, convenient floor cleaning is the order of the day, a disposable mop cloth may be the best solution. Swiffer offers this kit with the necessary pieces to get floors clean fast: the mop itself, four dry heavy-duty refills, three wet heavy-duty refills, 10 dry sweeping cloths, and two wet mopping pads. For the most part, we were impressed by this inexpensive, lightweight, and complete floor-cleaning system.

    In a recent development, swiffer’s 360-degree swivel action made hard-to-reach places easier to access, and its easy-grip handle kept the unit from slipping away while mopping. During tests, we found that the heavy-duty wet pad captured a lot of tough grime on our wood floors. (Note that these pads should not be used on unsealed wood floors.) On the downside, however, was the strong and somewhat lingering proprietary scent. Also, occasionally the pad popped out of the mophead for no apparent reason. Keep in mind that the wet refills should only be used to maintain sealed wood floors.

    Get the Swiffer mopping kit for wood floors at Amazon, Lowe’s, or Ace Hardware.

    Our Ratings: Ease of Use 3/5;Effectiveness 4/5; Maneuverability 4/5; Value 4/5.

    For those who are looking for an effective way to clean hardwood floors all in one step, a vac/mop combo may be the answer.

    The Tineco Floor ONE S5 smart wet/dry vacuum cleaner is an all-in-one machine. The unit vacuums up debris while mopping the floor simultaneously. It is self-propelled, which makes cleaning a breeze, especially anyone with arm or back issues.

    Safe for hardwood floors, the Tineco wet/dry vacuum cleaner uses its proprietary iLoop Smart Sensor Technology to automatically sense the level of dirt, which allows it to adjust suction, water flow, and brush-roller speed. When we tested it on a larger mess, the iLoop sensor properly sensed the soiled area and increased the roller speed. Once the area was clean, the iLoop sensor shifted the roller speed back down to normal.

    The cordless vacuum is battery-operated and runs up to 35 minutes on one charge. We found that this was plenty of time to clean our 1,700-square-foot home. We keep our floors pretty tidy and found that when we do so, the battery lasts even longer than 35 minutes.

    We were shocked to see how well this vac/mop cleaned our floors as evidenced by the feel of the floors on our bare feet and the dirty water in the tank. We’ve used many vac/mops throughout the years and we were so happy to see Tineco has a debris filter so hair and gunk does not fall to the bottom of the dirty-water tank.

    Another great feature is the large clean-water tank. We can clean our entire upstairs living area without having to stop and empty the dirty-water tank or refill the clean- water tank. This is a huge improvement over other vac/mops with smaller tanks.

    With its cordless design, this is our go-to mop for cleaning significant and small messes.

    Get the Tineco mop for wood floors at Amazon.

    Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5;Effectiveness 4/5; Maneuverability 5/5; Value 5/5.

    Industry observers note that we found this point-and-spray microfiber floor mop to be a hard-working weapon in the war on dirty hardwood floors. This spray mop comes prefilled with a full bottle of cleaner from Bona—a well-known brand in wood care—and a wide mophead designed to reduce the time spent cleaning. It’s a manual model, no cord or batteries are required, but it proved lightweight and maneuverable for easy mopping.

    Used dry, the microfiber cleaning pad did an excellent job of picking up dust and pet hair. To tackle stubborn dried messes, just pull the trigger to apply spray cleaner right where it’s needed. The clever built-in bumpers on the wide, long, rectangular mophead help prevent scratches on chair legs and baseboard molding. The reservoir for the cleaning solution is simple to refill, and the microfiber mop cloths are removable for machine washing.

    Sources indicate that expert recommended: Knoll regards Bona as a brand he trusts: “Without going to janitorial supply stores, the Bona microfiber floor mop is a top-notch choice and readily available. It balances efficiency with care for hardwood floors.”.

    Get the Bona mop for wood floors at Amazon, Ace Hardware, or Target.

    Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5;Effectiveness 5/5; Maneuverability 5/5; Value 5/5.

    Steam mopping offers a floor-cleaning solution that eliminates 99.9 percent of germs and bacteria without leaving behind any toxic residue. Recommended for hard, sealed floors, the Bissell PowerFresh steam mop has three steam settings and swivel steering for hard-to-reach spaces. The mop is safe for sealed hardwood and other flooring surfaces, and it comes with one microfiber soft pad, one microfiber scrubby pad, two fragrance discs, and a carpet glider.

    In user testing, this steam and microfiber mop was a real champ, capable of removing dried mud and ketchup. The fact that this tool creates steam to sanitize using water may be a boon to those with sensitivities to chemical cleaners. This steam mop has three steam settings for people to select from depending on the degree of stubborn dirt and stains, and the ample 23-foot power cord is a plus when cleaning large areas.

    Read our full review: Bissell 1940 PowerFresh Steam Mop for Wood Floors.

    Get the Bissell PowerFresh mop for wood floors at Amazon.

    Industry observers note that while we appreciated the light weight and convenient folding design of the foldable PurSteam 10-in-1 Steam Mop Cleaner, it could not compare with the Bissell 1940 PowerFresh mop for wood floors when it came to cleaning dried food and mud from our testing surfaces. Plus, its water reservoir didn’t empty completely (a potential for mold buildup), and its bundle of handheld steamer attachments came with no storage options.

    The O-Cedar ProMist Max Microfiber Spray Mop seemed promising with its unique wraparound flat mophead (akin to a mitten on the base of the mop). But in practice, it absorbed liquid (including its own cleaning fluid) poorly, and merely smeared dirt and dried ketchup around. We wanted to like its lightweight design, but it felt cheap and flimsy, particularly the trigger-spray handle.

    In a recent development, we put a series of mops for hardwood floors, both cordless and corded, through their paces in a typical home that accumulated dust, dirt, pet hair, and muddy paw prints. We used the mops with their provided cleaners or distilled water, as recommended by the manufacturers.

    In a recent development, we noted how easy or difficult the mops were to assemble, and considered the practicality of storing them. Finally, we used each in a controlled test of dried mud and ketchup smeared on hardwood floors and noted how much mess each floor mop left behind.

    It has been revealed that when purchasing a mop for wood flooring, think about its ease of use, any cleaning solutions it dispenses, and the price. In addition to the tool itself, factor in the size of the area that needs mopping. Here are some crucial considerations to look at when looking at mops for wood floors.

    It has been revealed that there are different types of mops available to suit various floor-maintenance preferences: flat mops, string mops, steam mops, and dust mops. Some are used exclusively for dusting floors, while other kinds function as both wet and dry mops.

    Old-fashioned dunk-in-a-bucket mops require hand-wringing, but there are more convenient, less-messy options today. These mops may feature electric or mechanical components for wringing, as well as either reusable or disposable parts, so look for the type and system that suits your cleaning preference, floor type, and floor size.

    The business end of a floor mop is typically either disposable or reusable. Disposable options are convenient for quick touch-ups and smaller floors, while reusable ones often prove more budget-friendly and can tackle larger surfaces.

    According to recent reports, both types of mopheads impact sustainability, but in different ways. Reusable mopheads require water and chemicals to launder after use, while disposable versions head straight to the landfill. For larger areas, a reusable, machine-washable mophead is probably more efficient and eco-friendly than using multiple disposable mopheads per cleaning session. Those who prefer a reusable option might consider microfiber mopheads, which will catch and hold dirt and liquids better than materials such as cotton or sponge while reducing the look of scratches and scuffs.

    In a recent development, according to Knoll, “Microfiber is the go-to. It’s soft, absorbent, and won’t damage your floors. It also wrings out well, keeping the water usage minimal.” He also added that microfiber mops are “great for picking up dust and fine particles without leaving scratches.”.

    According to recent reports, if pushing a manual mop around seems laborious and inefficient, consider an electric model. These products typically have a variety of cleaning modes and processes (including one specifically for wood floors), and may feature the use of steam and/or cleaning solutions. They often come with swiveling heads for easier maneuverability, too.

    Electric mops may be corded or cordless—and both types require access to an outlet. Corded mops must be plugged in during use, while the battery charger of cordless models must be plugged in as well. The portability of cordless models tends to appeal to folks who don’t want to be tied down to the length of a cord, typically because they have large areas to clean, and sometimes on different levels.

    When stubborn dirt and stains occur, wood floors may require more vigorous cleaning than just dry-mopping, but only with a product specifically formulated for hardwood flooring. While hardwood floors are usually finished and sealed, some versions may be unsealed—it’s important to avoid using water on unsealed hardwood floors, as well as harsh cleansers on any wood floor. An all-purpose floor cleaner, for instance, may dull or, worse, strip the finish.

    According to recent reports, though there are different types of cleaning solutions, those that can be used straight from the container without diluting tend to be safer, since any excess water from mixing a concentrated formula can seep into the wood and damage it. Some mops employ steam to clean and sanitize flooring, which should be safe for sealed hardwood—but to be safe, consult and follow all directions to avoid damage.

    Knoll recommends gentle cleaners: “Opt for pH-neutral, hardwood-specific cleaners to prevent damage.” Also, “damp mopping is the way. Ensure the mop is just moist enough to clean without leaving excess water.”.

    When it comes to mopping around furniture, under beds/sofas, and into hard-to-reach areas, maneuverability matters. A swivel-head mop is ideal for getting around obstacles. The shape of the mophead (circular, triangular, or rectangular) also impacts how easily it can access corners and tight spots.

    Mops may also include ergonomic features, some of which affect maneuvering, like telescoping handles to adjust length, and thereby extend reach. A poorly designed handle can also lead to arm and hand fatigue, so people will want to look for a model with a grip that feels good.

    Those who still want more information on cleaning hardwood flooring with a quality mop may find it here in the answers to some of the most common questions about this household chore.

    Mopping correctly can be a great way to maintain hardwood flooring, but using the wrong cleaning products can actually damage these expensive surfaces. A damp mop is often all that’s required to clean a hardwood floor; if the mop is too wet (with water or cleaning solution), excess liquid can seep into the cracks, causing the wood to warp.

    Sources indicate that cleaning a floor starts with removing dust and debris by sweeping, vacuuming, or dry-mopping. For stubborn dirt and stains, use a cleaner designed for the specific floor material, using a “less is more” approach according to the manufacturer’s directions. To mop a floor correctly, dip string or sponge mops in the cleaning fluid, wring it out, and then swab with the damp mop. Use plain water to do a final rinse if desired. Start mopping in a far corner of the room, moving in the direction of the grain on hardwood floors, and work your way to the door. When finished, rinse the mop and let it air dry or wash any reusable pads.

    In a recent development, swiffer’s heavy-duty pads are considered safe for linoleum, vinyl, laminate, and ceramic tile, as well as sealed wood, marble, and stone. They should not be used on unsealed wood floors. As with all floor cleaners, be cautious using any fluid on unfinished, damaged, or especially delicate materials.

    The National Wood Flooring Association recommends a heavy-duty mopping on wood floors monthly with a wood-flooring cleaner. However, it is safe to dry-mop daily or do a light mop on high-traffic areas once a week. For those without children and pets, feel free to give a very light mop on light-traffic areas more often.

    As the executive editor of Product Reviews, Stephanie Cronk has spent years researching and testing products. Cronk has been a pool owner for over 15 years and understands the importance of maintaining a clean pool in the warmer months. Besides her pool experience, Cronk also brings over 12 years of commerce experience to the BobVila.com team, where her focus is on reviewing and testing products in a variety of categories including DIY, home improvement, home appliances, outdoor living, and more.
